papers.abstract: Abstract IDH wild-type glioblastoma (GBM) is a common and incurable brain malignancy for which targeted therapies have shown limited clinical benefit. Tumor heterogeneity and cellular plasticity are major barriers to effective treatment, enabling tumor cells to evade therapy. Glioblastoma stem cells (GSCs) exist along a transcriptomic gradient between Developmental and Injury Response cellular states and exhibit substantial plasticity between these states. Defining the mechanisms that regulate GSC heterogeneity and plasticity may reveal new therapeutic opportunities. To identify subtype-specific vulnerabilities, we performed CRISPR-Cas9 fitness screens across 30 patient-derived GSC cultures. Clustering of screening results recapitulated the Developmental–Injury Response gradient and revealed distinct genetic dependencies. Developmental GSCs depended on neurodevelopmental transcription factors including OLIG2, SOX2, NFIB, and SALL1, whereas Injury Response GSCs depended on integrin and focal adhesion signaling genes including PTK2, ILK, and ITGB1. These dependencies conferred differential sensitivity to inhibitors targeting β1 integrin, focal adhesion kinase, MEK, and OLIG2, highlighting opportunities for precision targeting of defined GSC subtypes. To identify regulators of GSC cell-state identity, we performed FACS-based phenotypic CRISPR knockout screens using marker genes associated with the Injury Response and Developmental states. These screens uncovered epigenetic and transcriptional regulatory networks required for maintenance of GSC state identity. Notably, loss of P300 expression or activity suppressed the Injury Response transcriptional program and impaired self-renewal, invasion, and tumor initiation. Leveraging these candidate regulators, we performed single-cell CRISPR screening (scCRISPR-seq) to generate high-resolution transcriptional profiles following perturbation of state regulators across a diverse panel of GSC cultures. Together, these findings define molecular dependencies underlying GBM heterogeneity and identify regulatory mechanisms governing GSC plasticity, providing a framework for the development of state-targeting therapeutic strategies.

papers.abstract: Abstract While immunotherapies have achieved durable responses in several cancers, they have failed to provide significant benefit in glioblastoma (GBM). This is partly driven by stem-like, immune-silent tumor states that limit immune recognition. The tumor-intrinsic epigenetic programs that maintain these immune-evasive states remain poorly understood. Here, we functionally investigated factors involved in the epigenetic maintenance of immune-suppressive tumor cell states. We evaluated bulk, single-cell, and spatial transcriptomic reference datasets to identify associations between immune-suppressive programs and epigenetic regulatory elements. Our analysis revealed that CHK2, YBX1 and EZH2 expressions were positively correlated with one another, enriched within immune-silent tumor cell states, and spatially localized to immunologically cold regions of GBM tumors. Protein expression studies across glioma models further indicated that CHK2, YBX1 and EZH2 were functionally interconnected, as genetic disruption of one component altered the expression of the others within the axis. We therapeutically targeted this network using GSK126 and SU056, inhibitors of EZH2 and CHK2-YBX1 signaling, respectively. Treatment with GSK126 or SU056 independently increased the expression of key immune-recognition markers, including MHC-I, MHC-II and PD-L1 in GBM cells. These findings suggested that EZH2 inhibition shifted GBM cells away from an immune-silent state toward a more immune-visible phenotype. Collectively, this work identified EZH2 as an epigenetic regulator of the CHK2-YBX1 immune-suppressive signaling hub that we had previously described in GBM. These findings may provide a promising framework for reprogramming GBM cells toward immune visibility and for developing epigenetic and transcriptional biomarkers to guide future immunotherapy combinations.

papers.abstract: Abstract Tumor-associated neutrophils (TANs) are emerging regulators of glioblastoma (GBM) immunity, yet the mechanisms that induce tolerogenic pro-tumoral states remain poorly defined. We investigated whether GBM cells act as mitochondrial redistribution hubs, acquiring mitochondria from stromal and immune compartments and redeploying them into neutrophils to reprogram innate immunity. We utilized global mitochondrial reporter mice, purified pup-derived reporter astrocytes, orthotopic CT-2A, GL261 models, U87 systems, adoptive transfer, confocal microscopy with 3D reconstruction, electron microscopy, flow cytometry, Seahorse, SCENITH, single-cell RNA-seq, myeloid knockout models, and survival studies. MIRO1-dependent mitochondrial trafficking was targeted using an institutionally developed intracranial MIRO1-reducer hydrogel. GBM cells acquired mitochondria from purified primary astrocytes and immune cells and then re-donated these same mitochondria to infiltrating neutrophils in vitro and in vivo. Astrocytes isolated from global reporter pups donated mitochondria to CT2A and GL261 cells; these same astrocyte-derived mitochondria were subsequently transferred by GBM cells into neutrophils, increasing neutrophil CD39 expression (**P < 0.01). This sequential mitochondrial relay was validated using a GFP-tagged mitochondrial complex V reporter mice, Mitochondria-recipient neutrophils acquired a suppressive immunometabolic phenotype, with increased SER51, TREM2, APOE, and PD-L1 in U87 and CT2A systems (***P < 0.001). Human scRNA-seq identified discrete TAN states enriched for mitochondrial transfer-response signatures within pro-tumoral and exhausted neutrophil programs. Seahorse and SCENITH demonstrated that tumor-neutrophil interaction rewired metabolic coupling, significantly altering basal respiration, maximal respiration, spare respiratory capacity, glycolysis, and glycolytic capacity (***P < 0.001 to ****P < 0.0001), with selected ATP-production differences also observed. MIRO1 reducer suppressed TAN exhaustion, reducing APOE, TREM2, and PD-L1, and institution-derived human GBM scRNA-seq further showed attenuation of SPP1-associated myeloid and mitochondrial-stress programs. In CT2A-bearing mice, intracranial MIRO1 reducer hydrogel combined with anti-PD-1 significantly prolonged survival (log-rank P < 0.0001). Together, these findings establish, to our knowledge, the first evidence that glioblastoma converts host-derived mitochondria into transferable immune-instructive signals, defining an organelle-level paradigm of non-cell-autonomous cancer biology that reprograms host immune fate and enforces inducible tolerance.

papers.abstract: Abstract Glioblastoma (GBM) is a heterogenous and malignant brain tumor that hijacks neural circuits to fuel its own growth and invasion. Although paracrine and synaptic signaling are known drivers of GBM progression, these interactions have largely been studied without considering the profound regional diversity of the human CNS. As glioma cells interact with anatomically distinct neural tracts during disease progression, there is a need to examine how region-specific microenvironments differentially shape invasive GBM cell states and neuron-tumor connections. To address this in a fully human model, we engrafted patient-derived GBM cells into human induced pluripotent stem cell-derived organoids patterned to forebrain, midbrain, and spinal cord identities. Intriguingly, we found that GBM cells were far more infiltrative in forebrain organoids than spinal cord organoids. Single-cell RNA sequencing revealed that, across all regional contexts, GBM cells were depleted in an astrocyte-like state and enriched in a neuron/glia progenitor-like (NPC-like) state. NPC-like GBM cells were primed along a neuron-like lineage, and tumors initially enriched in NPC-like cells prior to engraftment achieved greater organoid coverage, suggesting greater infiltration and integration of this cell type within neural tissues. However, because this NPC-like enrichment was conserved across distinct regional organoids, inter-regional differences in tumor invasion could not be explained by divergent GBM cell state signatures. These findings instead prompted us to investigate the identities of tumor-extrinsic neuronal partners using monosynaptic retrograde tracing. We discovered that GBM cells in the forebrain received synaptic input from deep-layer TBR1+ excitatory neurons, which normally send long-range projections outside the cerebral cortex into subcortical regions such as the thalamus. In contrast, GBM cells in spinal cord organoids preferentially received synaptic input from inhibitory interneurons. Collectively, our data suggest that circuit-specific neuron-tumor interactions differentially shape GBM invasion across distinct regions and may represent therapeutically targetable mechanisms in glioblastoma.

papers.abstract: Abstract Primary central nervous system lymphoma (PCNSL) is a CNS-restricted lymphoma with poor prognosis. Despite sharing pathological features with systemic diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (DLBCL), PCNSL exhibits unique molecular mutation patterns, highlighting the critical role of the intracranial tumor microenvironment (TME). However, the role of microglia within TME remains poorly understood. Here, integrative analysis of single-cell transcriptomic data from systemic DLBCL and PCNSL reveals a distinct TME in PCNSL characterized by a heightened immunosuppressive state via microglia. Here, we identify a subpopulation of ARG1+ microglia enriched in the PCNSL tumor core, representing activated morphology and reduced branching complexity. Functionally, these microglia exhibit enhanced cytokine secretion via upgrading PI3K-AKT signal pathway, thereby remodeling the TME and ultimately promoting tumor progression. Targeting this microglia subtype with resveratrol, a bioactive small molecule, resulted in significant tumor suppression in vivo and vitro, accompanied by reduced expression of immunosuppressive cytokines and functional reprogramming of microglia. Collectively, our findings identify ARG1+ microglia as key orchestrators of the immunosuppressive TME in PCNSL through secretion cytokine and highlight microglia-targeted modulation by resveratrol as a potential therapeutic strategy.

papers.abstract: Abstract Diffuse hemispheric glioma, H3G34-mutant (DHG-H3G34), is a rare and highly aggressive pediatric high-grade glioma with poor prognosis and limited therapeutic options. These tumors are thought to arise from interneuron progenitors and comprise malignant cell states that recapitulate normal interneuron development, ranging from stem-like radial glia/NPC-like populations to more differentiated INPC-like and eIN-like states. Unlike diffuse midline glioma (DMG), in which proliferating cells are largely confined to a single OPC-like cell state, DHG-H3G34 contains a heterogeneous proliferative compartment spanning multiple tumor cell states, suggesting that proliferation may be regulated in a cell-state-specific manner. We therefore investigated the intrinsic and extrinsic programs regulating proliferation in DHG-H3G34, focusing on the neuronal tumor microenvironment. Single-cell transcriptomic analyses of patient tumor samples revealed distinct cycling programs across malignant cell states, including differential expression of genes involved in neuronal communication. Together, these observations suggest that DHG-H3G34 may differ from DMG in both the expression of neuronal signaling-related genes and the way tumor cells respond to neuronal cues, in line with its distinct developmental lineage and cell-state architecture. To test this experimentally, we used multiple patient-derived DHG-H3G34 cell lines and neuron–tumor co-culture models to evaluate the effects of neuronal signals on tumor cell states and its specific cycling dynamics, using DMG as a comparative framework. Collectively, this work supports a model in which lineage identity and cellular state shape neuron-tumor interactions in DHG-H3G34 and may expose subtype-specific therapeutic vulnerabilities.

papers.abstract: Abstract Glioblastoma (GBM) remains the deadliest and most treatment-resistant brain tumor, with median patient survival remaining only 14-16 months despite aggressive therapies. A major challenge in improving patient outcomes is the profound intratumoral heterogeneity, cellular plasticity, and adaptive resistance mechanisms that drive tumor recurrence. Recent single-cell and multi-omics studies have revealed that GBM cells occupy dynamic transcriptional states resembling neurodevelopmental lineages, which can transition in response to microenvironmental cues and therapeutic pressure, contributing to tumor evolution and resistance. However, the epigenetic and genetic mechanisms that sustain these stem/progenitor-like tumor programs remain poorly understood. The Epidermal Growth Factor Receptor (EGFR) pathway plays critical roles in regulating stem/progenitor-like states during neurodevelopment and is among the most frequently altered pathways in GBM. Previous work from our lab demonstrated that the transcriptional co-activators YAP/TAZ are upregulated downstream of EGFR signaling in EGFR-amplified/mutant GBM, where they function as key regulators of tumor growth. Inhibition of YAP/TAZ-TEAD activity in patient-derived GBM models induces apoptosis and growth arrest, underscoring their importance in tumor maintenance. Building on these findings, we hypothesize that targeting YAP/TAZ-TEAD signaling will disrupt heterogeneous transcriptional states that sustain tumor progression, self-renewal, and therapeutic resistance. To test this hypothesis, we employ iPSC-derived human brain organoids that recapitulate the neural microenvironment and engraft them with EGFR-mutant patient-derived GBM stem cells. These engrafted organoids are treated with YAP/TAZ-TEAD inhibitors and subsequently processed for single-cell RNA sequencing to identify associated transcriptional changes. Ongoing studies focus on identifying GBM-specific transcriptional targets and epigenetic mechanisms that drive intratumoral heterogeneity and therapeutic response and resistance, with the goal of discovering biomarkers predictive of treatment response in EGFR-mutant GBM. Collectively, this work lays the foundation for developing YAP/TAZ-TEAD targeted therapeutic strategies aimed at improving clinical outcomes for patients with GBM.

papers.abstract: Abstract Neurons within the brain tumor microenvironment play a major role in shaping tumor behavior. Recent landmark studies demonstrated that GABAergic interneurons form tumor-promoting synapses with diffuse midline glioma (DMG) cells. Because DMG cells express high levels of the chloride importer NKCC1 and low levels of the chloride exporter KCC2, GABA signaling becomes depolarizing rather than inhibitory, driving tumor growth. While these findings were established in mouse xenograft models, how chloride dysregulation operates across human DMG cell states and whether restoring chloride homeostasis can therapeutically suppress tumor progression remains largely unknown. To address these questions, we use our recently published MiCBO-TF platform (Sarnow & Tang et al., Neuro-Oncology, 2025), the first neuroimmune-competent all-human brain tumor organoid model incorporating patient-derived DMG cells, interneurons, astrocytes, and microglia. This system enables the investigation of tumor-neural interactions in a human brain tissue context inaccessible to xenograft approaches. Using scRNA-seq analysis of patient biopsies, we confirmed an NKCC1-high/KCC2-low expression pattern across DMG cell states. In parallel, GCaMP imaging in MiCBO-TF organoids demonstrated robust depolarizing calcium responses to GABA in DMG cells. Strikingly, we found that the FLT3 kinase inhibitor KW-2449, previously identified in our epilepsy studies as a potent inducer of neuronal KCC2 expression, also elevates KCC2 in DMG cells and suppresses tumor sphere growth, revealing a conserved chloride regulatory pathway shared between neurons and tumor cells. Ongoing studies combining gramicidin-perforated patch clamp recording with genetically encoded chloride and calcium imaging are mapping GABA signaling polarity across distinct DMG subpopulations in both neuron co-culture and human organoid systems. Together, this work establishes a new therapeutic framework in pediatric neuro-oncology: restoring inhibitory GABAergic signaling through chloride homeostasis correction as a neuro-compatible strategy to suppress brain tumor growth.

papers.abstract: Abstract Diffuse hemispheric gliomas harboring the H3G34 mutation (DHG-H3G34-mutant) are lethal malignancies primarily affecting adolescents and young adults. Recent findings indicate these tumors exhibit marked intra-tumoral heterogeneity, harboring transcriptional programs that mimic interneuron development. These range from progenitor states to mature Astrocytic-like/Mesenchymal-like (AC-like/Mes-like) and early GABAergic Interneuron-like (eIN-like) cells. Because normal GABAergic interneurons orchestrate rhythmic communication network dynamics—a process known to drive glioma proliferation—we hypothesized that eIN-like tumor subpopulations hijack neural network circuits to fuel tumor progression. To correlate network activity with specific transcriptional states, we integrated live-cell calcium imaging with in situ spatial transcriptomics. A primary DHG-H3G34-mutant cell line expressing the genetically encoded calcium indicator GCAMP8s was cultured and recorded for 5 minutes on a Xenium slide to characterize network dynamics. Following imaging, the cells were fixed and analyzed using a custom 10x Xenium panel specifically designed for DHG-H3G34-mutant cell program annotation. Live-cell calcium imaging identified three distinct modes of network communication within the DHG-H3G34-mutant models: (1) no detectable calcium transients, (2) slow rhythmic and arrhythmic communication (<10 mHz), and (3) fast rhythmic and arrhythmic communication (11-100 mHz). Subsequent in situ spatial transcriptomic mapping revealed a correlation between signaling frequency and cell state. Cells exhibiting high-frequency calcium communication were exclusively restricted to the more mature AC-like/Mes-like and eIN-like transcriptional programs. In contrast, low-frequency signaling and the absence of calcium transients were distributed across all DHG-H3G34-mutant cellular programs. DHG-H3G34-mutant tumors utilize diverse transcriptional programs to drive aggressive progression. While rhythmic calcium activity promotes tumor growth in adult glioblastomas, our findings demonstrate that DHG-H3G34-mutant cells exhibit calcium transients at significantly higher frequencies. By mapping these high-frequency network dynamics specifically to mature eIN-like and AC-like subpopulations, this study elucidates novel oncogenic mechanisms and highlights potential subtype-specific vulnerabilities in pediatric and young adult gliomas.

papers.abstract: Abstract Glioblastoma (GB), the most aggressive primary brain tumor in adults, is characterized by striking intratumoral heterogeneity and diffuse invasion of the brain parenchyma. The subcellular mechanisms underlying this invasive behavior have remained largely elusive. However, whole-brain colonization is driven in part by so-called tumor microtubes (TMs), neurite-like protrusions formed by a distinct subpopulation of GB cells. Our work identifies local protein translation within these TMs as a previously underappreciated driver of glioblastoma invasion. By combining subcellular organelle organization and spatial transcriptomics with functional readouts, we demonstrate that TM gene expression is a key determinant of invasive cell identity. Strikingly, these invasive cells show significantly enhanced local translation within TMs, mirroring translation dynamics known from axonal growth cones during neurodevelopment. Functional perturbation of TM-localized translation using photoswitchable puromycin, alongside targeted knockdowns of the TM-enriched proteins GPM6A and GAP43, demonstrates that local translation is an active driver of TM dynamics, invasion, and tumor growth. These findings define local translation as a key determinant of glioblastoma invasion and tumor heterogeneity, and open new avenues for therapeutic targeting.

papers.abstract: Abstract Diffuse midline glioma (DMG) is a devastating pediatric cancer that hijacks surrounding neurons to promote tumor proliferation via neuron–glioma synapses. Emerging evidence indicates that neural circuits influence DMG growth through glutamatergic, GABAergic, cholinergic, and serotonergic signaling. Here, we report that adrenergic signaling, specifically through the β2-adrenergic receptor (ADRB2), strongly influences the immune compartment of the tumor microenvironment (TME) in an allograft mouse model of DMG. Wildtype (wt) mice, or mice lacking Adrb2 (Adrb2KO), were orthotopically implanted with H3K27M-mutant, IUE-derived DMG cells into the pons, followed by bulk and single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq). Although the absence of ADRB2 did not alter DMG growth, bulk RNA sequencing of endpoint tumors (5–6 weeks) revealed 489 differentially expressed genes (p value and FDR < 0.05 and FC > 2) in tumors grafted in Adrb2KO mice compared to wt. Interestingly, we saw increased expression of neuronal signaling genes and decreased expression of immunosuppressive genes in Adrb2KO group . To investigate cell type–specific effects when ADRB2 is lost from host animals, we performed scRNA-seq of mid-stage (3 weeks) and late-stage (5-weeks post-engraftment) tumors. Pseudobulk RNA analysis of all cells showed increased expression of inflammatory and T cell exhaustion–associated genes, including Cxcl13 and Timd4, alongside downregulation of immunosuppressive genes such as CD5L and Arg1. Furthermore, consensus non-negative matrix factorization (cNMF) of myeloid populations revealed a marked reduction in Arg1+ immunoregulatory programs in tumors from Adrb2KO mice. Together, these findings suggest that loss of ADRB2 enhances inflammation and reduces immunosuppression in DMG, a tumor type typically considered immunologically “cold.” Efforts are now focused on assessing whether pharmacological blockade of ADRB2 could improve the efficacy of existing immunotherapy strategies by shifting DMG tumors from an immunosuppressive to an inflammatory state.

papers.abstract: Abstract Background H3 G34-mutant diffuse hemispheric glioma (DHG) is an aggressive brain tumor with no curative therapy. Younger age is a poor prognostic factor, but the underlying biological mechanism is unknown. We hypothesize that tumor cell states and tumor microenvironment (TME) composition differ across the age spectrum and that these differences correlate with treatment response and patient outcomes. Methods Paired transcriptome and DNA methylome of diagnostic samples from 31 newly diagnosed DHG patients in a multi-institutional cohort were deconvoluted using a scRNA-seq reference cohort (N = 19). Cox regression assessed progression-free survival (PFS) and overall survival (OS) in age-stratified analyses (<16 vs. ≥16 years) and in temozolomide (TMZ)-adjusted models with age×cell type interaction term; statistical significance p < 0.05 by both platforms was required. Results The median age at diagnosis was 15 years (10-28 years). The median PFS was 0.90 years (95%CI:0.59-1.54), and the median OS was 1.95 years (95%CI:1.24-4.34). Substantial inter-tumoral heterogeneity was observed in malignant cell states and TME populations, while radial glia-like tumor cells and myeloid cells predominated. Higher astrocyte (AC)-like abundance correlated with inferior PFS in patients <16 years but with superior OS in patients ≥16 years. Conversely, oligodendrocyte abundance correlated with superior PFS in patients <16 years but with inferior OS in patients ≥16 years. Higher early interneuron (eIN)-like and AC+mesenchymal (MES)-like abundance were associated with superior OS in patients ≥16. Crucially, TMZ treatment provided consistent PFS benefit despite heterogeneous effects of specific TME elements and tumor cell states. Conclusions Our findings provide evidence of the age-dependent biological differences in DHG. We demonstrate that the prognostic impact of specific tumor cell states and TME elements reverses across the age spectrum. These results suggest a cellular basis for age-specific DHG prognosis. Elucidating the roles of the identified cell types and their interactions can help identify cell-specific vulnerabilities as therapeutic targets.

papers.abstract: Abstract Glioblastoma (GBM) is the most common and lethal primary brain tumor in adults, with a five-year survival rate of only 7%. Its aggressive progression is driven by both intrinsic tumor properties and dynamic interactions within the tumor microenvironment, where astrocytes are a major cellular component. Despite their critical roles in regulating synaptic function and maintaining brain homeostasis, how astrocytes functionally contribute to GBM progression remains a fundamental knowledge gap. Using an in utero electroporation-based mouse model (IUE-GBM), single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) identified a distinct cluster of tumor-associated astrocytes (TAAs) with downregulated calcium signaling-associated genes in late-stage compared to early-stage GBM. Analysis of human GBM scRNA-seq data confirmed significant dysregulation of astrocyte calcium signaling pathways in TAAs relative to astrocytes in healthy controls, and two-photon imaging of awake tumor-bearing mice validated that tumor-associated astrocytes exhibit reduced calcium activity in vivo, suggesting astrocyte calcium activity decreases during tumor progression. Chemogenetic stimulation of astrocyte calcium (As-GqDREADD) significantly reduced tumor size and proliferation and extended median survival in IUE-GBM mice, with similar effects observed in a patient-derived xenograft model using IDH-wildtype GBM cells (PDX-GBM). Conversely, attenuation of astrocyte calcium using the CalEx system significantly increased tumor size and proliferation, demonstrating that astrocyte calcium bidirectionally regulates GBM growth. To identify the underlying mechanism, conditioned media from GqDREADD-stimulated primary astrocytes inhibited glioma cell proliferation and migration in vitro, implicating astrocyte-secreted factors as mediators. Mass spectrometry identified Serping1 as a top candidate, which was elevated in As-GqDREADD stimulated tumors in vivo and was sufficient to inhibit GBM proliferation in vitro. These findings demonstrate that astrocyte calcium signaling plays a central role in regulating GBM growth and identify astrocyte-secreted factors as novel therapeutic targets for this devastating and incurable cancer.

papers.abstract: Abstract Glioblastoma (GBM) remains an intractable malignancy with modest therapeutic improvements and dismal patient prognosis. It is increasingly recognized that GBM cells do not grow in isolation but actively engage the brain’s neuronal circuitry. While neuron-to-glioma synaptic-like communication promotes tumor progression, whether glioma cells hijack neuronal proteins for tumor–tumor or neuron–tumor pseudo-synaptic interactions remains largely unresolved. In the normal brain, TSPAN13 is expressed predominantly in neurons and implicated in synapse adhesion and organization. In contrast, we demonstrate robust TSPAN13 overexpression in glioblastoma, where elevated TSPAN13 levels correlate significantly with reduced patient survival. We overexpressed TSPAN13 in GL261 and U87 glioma cells, which significantly accelerated proliferation and migration, whereas CRISPR/Cas9-mediated knockout produced the opposite effect. Co-culture with primary mouse neurons showed that TSPAN13 overexpression significantly increased synapse formation and calcium transients, while knockout decreased both, indicating TSPAN13 promotes neuron–tumor functional connectivity. Bulk RNA-seq of TSPAN13-overexpressing glioma cells revealed enrichment of genes for synapse assembly, synaptic transmission, and glutamatergic signaling. These findings support that TSPAN13 facilitates both neuron–tumor and tumor–tumor synaptic-like communication. Single-cell RNA sequencing and spatial transcriptomics pinpointed TSPAN13 to a neural-progenitor-cell (NPC)-like glioma subpopulation that co-expresses synaptic signatures, with spatial mapping confirming co‑localization with glutamatergic synapse markers. GCaMP6s calcium imaging showed TSPAN13-overexpressing U87 cells exhibit significantly enhanced KCl-evoked calcium transients, mimicking neuronal excitability. This aberrant electrical activity was effectively suppressed by the AMPA receptor antagonist Perampanel, confirming AMPA receptor involvement. In a syngeneic GL261-C57BL/6 orthotopic model, TSPAN13-overexpressing tumors grew faster and shortened survival, effects significantly attenuated by systemic Perampanel. Collectively, our results support a model in which glioma cells co-opt TSPAN13 to facilitate AMPA receptor-dependent pseudo-synaptic communication among tumor cells and with neurons, thereby contributing to a self-reinforcing loop that drives GBM progression. Pharmacological blockade with Perampanel validated this dependence on AMPA receptor-mediated transmission and provides a preclinical basis for disrupting oncogenic synaptic mimicry in GBM.

papers.abstract: Abstract Recent studies identified bi-directional communication between neurons and glioma tumors as a key driver of hyperexcitability and tumor growth. While much of this work has focused on the activity of excitatory neurons, roles for inhibitory neurons remain poorly defined. We analyzed publicly available human glioma datasets along with internal single-cell RNA sequencing of glioma samples to influence studies in an autochthonous murine glioma model. We utilized this model to complete an in-vivo screen, alter specific gene expression, conduct electroencephalogram (EEG) recordings, record tonic GABA levels, visualize GABA activity with a fluorescent reporter, assess proliferation with BrdU pulse, and deploy a chemogenetic system to modulate activity of inhibitory neurons. Through an in-vivo screen, we found that loss of a GABA transporter (Slc6a1LOF) enhanced glioma progression (85 vs.102 days, p-val=0.0004), while simultaneously increasing network hyperactivity detected on EEG. Furthermore, Slc6a1LOF reduced tonic GABA release by tumors and reduced GABA fluorescent reporter activity (p-val=0.00044 and p-val=0.0126). Tumoral GABA production was found to be dependent on Maob, where Maob overexpression enhanced GABA fluorescent reporter activity (p-val=0.0038). Ipsilateral inhibitory neuronal activity induced proliferative changes in glioma with chemogenetic activation suppressing (p-val=0.0148) and inhibition enhancing glioma proliferation (p-val=0.0041). Gliomas overexpress Diazepam Binding Inhibitory (DBI), a secreted negative allosteric modulator of GABA-A. DBI overexpression (DBIOE) enhanced tumor growth (84 vs. 102 days, p-val=0.0141) and exacerbated tumor-related hyperexcitability on EEG, serving as a link between glioma related modulation of inhibitory neurons and proliferation. The proliferative effect of DBIOE was abrogated by activation of ipsilateral inhibitory neurons (p-val=0.9917). Additionally, overexpression of just the GABA binding residues of DBI recapitulated the same enhanced growth as DBIOE (87 vs. 84 days, p-val=0.2802). Collectively, our findings indicate that glioma tumors utilize multiple mechanisms to manipulate the activity of inhibitory neurons as a means to drive network hyperactivity, which ultimately facilitates malignant expansion.

papers.abstract: Abstract Over 2,000 adults are diagnosed annually with isocitrate dehydrogenase-mutant (IDHm) glioma. These tumors recur despite treatment, driven by extensive cellular heterogeneity. However, most molecular studies rely on single biopsies, failing to capture spatial diversity. We applied spatially informed 3D whole tumor sampling to profile 324 samples from 32 IDHm gliomas using exome (n = 323), RNA (n = 318), ATAC (n = 92), and Hi-C (n = 14) sequencing. Integrating 3D spatial coordinates with multi-omic analysis revealed that tumor purity decreased with distance from the tumor centroid (R=-0.32, p = 2.8 × 10-8), while inter-sample genomic (R = 0.24, p = 8.1x10-15), transcriptomic (R = 0.12, p = 1.0x10-5), and epigenetic (R = 0.13, p = 5.0x10-13) similarity increased with spatial proximity. This radial organization was unique to IDHm tumors compared to IDH-wildtype glioblastoma. Covariation network analysis identified groups of coordinated transcriptomic and epigenomic features. We annotated these networks using single-cell RNA and ATAC-sequencing cell atlases, motif enrichment, and correlations with tumor purity and spatial localization. This analysis recovered and significantly extended known tumor-intrinsic and microenvironmental states, including glial-progenitor-like tumor cells, astrocytoma-specific inflammation, and oligodendroglioma-associated neuronal hijacking, and revealed their spatial organization. Notably, in contrast to glioblastoma and astrocytoma, neuronal hijacking networks in oligodendroglioma were enriched towards the tumor core (R=-0.33, p = 2.5 × 10-2) instead of the periphery, suggesting distinct mechanisms of neurite recruitment. Projection of these programs onto IDHm tumors from TCGA (n = 415) revealed an astrocytoma-specific survival association driven by mature oligodendrocyte-related signatures identified independently by expression (HR = 10.21, p = 4.5x10-3) and open chromatin programs (HR = 5.43, p = 3.3 x10-3). Higher expression was associated with worse survival across multiple oligodendrocyte networks, implicating increased oligodendrocyte content—rather than a specific functional cell phenotype—in poor clinical outcome for astrocytoma patients. We conclude that multi-omic profiling across whole tumors reveals clinically relevant tumor architecture and new microenvironmental features with prognostic significance.

papers.abstract: Abstract Recurrent glioblastoma (GBM) emerges after surgery, radiotherapy, and temozolomide within a tissue environment shaped by treatment effects, injury, hypoxia and inflammation. Although recent spatial studies have defined the architecture of GBM, how this architecture is remodeled during therapy-shaped recurrence remains poorly understood. To address this, 10x Visium HD spatial transcriptomic profiling was applied to paired GBM cohort from GLASS consortium including 28 patients, with 27 matched primary-recurrent pairs and one patient with primary samples only. To resolve tumor-intrinsic, microenvironmental, and mixed/interface signals, we developed a layered consensus annotation framework integrating copy number derived malignancy calls, celltype deconvolution, lineage marker gene scoring and tumor functional state scores to classify malignant, non-malignant, and tumor microenvironment interface compartments. Neighborhood enrichment scores were then used to determine which tumor and microenvironmental compartments became spatially associated or separated at recurrence, while non-negative matrix factorization was used to identify malignant and interface-associated transcriptional programs enriched in primary versus recurrent disease. Neighborhood enrichment showed recurrence-associated rewiring between tumor compartments and myeloid, vascular/stromal, and glial regions. Preliminary NES patterns suggested that some recurrent tumors acquire increased AC-MES tumor-state admixture and enhanced proximity between tumor compartments and SPP1 or C3 associated myeloid programs, although these patterns varied across matched pairs, supporting patient-specific spatial trajectories of recurrence. NMF of pure malignant bins identified recurrent enriched stress and remodeling programs, including MES-like hypoxia, inflammatory myeloid-associated, and vascular/ECM-like signatures, while primary-enriched programs showed more developmental, neural, and astrocytic-like features. NMF including interface bins further highlighted boundary-associated programs linking malignant adaptation to remodeled microenvironmental niches. Together, these findings extend recent spatial GBM studies by measuring how tumor architecture changes from primary to recurrent disease within the same patients, supporting a model in which recurrent GBM evolves through patient-specific malignant adaptation within a post-treatment spatial microenvironment.

papers.abstract: Abstract Glioblastoma (GBM) is an aggressive brain tumor characterized by extensive invasion, therapeutic resistance, and a highly dynamic tumor microenvironment. Rap1b, a small GTPase, has been implicated in cancer progression; however, its functional role in GBM remains incompletely defined. In this study, we performed RNA sequencing in U87MG glioblastoma cells following Rap1b knockdown to systematically investigate its regulatory functions. Differential expression analysis revealed widespread transcriptomic alterations, with over 5,000 genes significantly dysregulated. Functional enrichment analyses demonstrated that Rap1b regulates gene programs associated with innate immune-like responses, vesicle-mediated secretion, and cell adhesion dynamics, including neutrophil activation, leukocyte degranulation, and focal adhesion pathways. Gene set enrichment analysis further identified Rap1b-dependent modulation of key oncogenic pathways, including VEGF signaling, TGF-β signaling, focal adhesion, and chemokine signaling, indicating a role in tumor-microenvironment interactions and invasion. To extend these findings, we analyzed publicly available single-cell RNA-seq data and found that RAP1B expression is positively correlated with tumor invasion and interferon response signatures in neoplastic cells, supporting its functional relevance in GBM progression. Importantly, several Rap1b-associated genes exhibited significant correlations with patient survival and showed differential expression across glioma grades, highlighting their clinical significance. Collectively, our findings demonstrate that Rap1b drives GBM progression through coordinated regulation of immune-associated transcriptional programs, adhesion signaling, and tumor invasiveness, suggesting that Rap1b may represent a potential therapeutic target in glioblastoma.

papers.abstract: Abstract Brain metastases are a common and devastating complication of cancer and remain largely incurable, with limited understanding of the timing of metastatic spread and the mechanisms enabling adaptation to the brain microenvironment. We assembled a large-scale single-cell atlas comprising 558 tumor samples from 539 patients, including 287 intracranial and 271 extracranial tumors across 14 cancer types, integrating 141 newly generated samples with 417 curated samples from 16 studies, including matched longitudinal primary–metastasis pairs. Phylogenetic reconstruction revealed two major metastatic trajectories: most brain metastases were consistent with early dissemination followed by independent evolution, while a minority reflected late dissemination from advanced primary clones. These trajectories were associated with distinct genomic features, including enrichment of MYC gain in early dissemination and EGFR gain in late dissemination, and correlated with time to metastatic progression. Transcriptionally, we identified a spectrum of malignant cell states, including a previously unrecognized neuronal-like program enriched in intracranial metastases, characterized by glutamatergic signaling and increased proliferative activity, consistent with adaptation to the neural niche. The brain metastatic microenvironment was distinct, with a myeloid-dominant immune composition, coordinated hypoxia programs across malignant and immune compartments, and reduced antigen presentation signatures. Notably, neuronal-like malignant states were inversely correlated with MHC class II expression in antigen-presenting cells, suggesting a coordinated tumor–immune axis of immune evasion. Integrative analysis supports a brain-specific ecosystem linking neuronal-like malignant programs, immunosuppressive myeloid states, hypoxia, and neurotrophin-associated stromal features. These findings indicate that brain metastases frequently arise from early dissemination and adopt neuro-adaptive and immune-evasive programs that may support growth in the brain, providing a framework for therapeutic targeting.

papers.abstract: Abstract Diffuse midline gliomas (DMGs) are among the most lethal pediatric brain tumors and exhibit substantial intratumoral heterogeneity. Malignant cell hierarchy spans from stalled stem-like oligodendrocyte progenitor (OPC-like) to more differentiated astrocyte (AC-like) and oligodendrocyte (OC-like) programs, in addition to mesenchymal (MES-like) features. The dynamic coexistence of these cellular states contributes to therapeutic resistance in other high-grade gliomas, yet their clinical impact in DMG remains understudied. Here, we spatially profiled a unique cohort of histone 3 lysine 27-to-methionine (H3K27M)-mutant DMG patients enrolled in PNOC022 DMG-ACT (DMG-Adaptive Combination Trial) to assess how cellular composition and spatial architecture relate to clinical outcome and response to dordaviprone (ONC201) and paxalisib (PI3K inhibitor). A total of 48 biopsy sections obtained prior to radiotherapy, including 10 H3K27M-mutant DMG patients post-treatment (6 post-dordaviprone, 4 post-paxalisib) and 8 pre-treatment cores, were profiled using imaging-based spatial transcriptomics (Xenium 5K, 10x Genomics). This approach enabled the capture of ∼1 million spatially resolved cells and identification of malignant states (OPC-like, AC-like, OC-like, MES-like, and cycling) alongside non-malignant populations in situ. Spatial analysis revealed non-random organization of malignant states, with OPC-like cells preferentially co-localizing with cycling populations, while AC-like and OC-like states were spatially anticorrelated. Importantly, the relative abundance of specific cellular states at diagnosis was associated with patient outcomes. In this cohort, AC-like cells (GFAP+) were significantly enriched in short-term survivors (OR = 2.64, 95% CI: [2.58–2.69], Fisher’s exact p < 0.001), while OC-like cells (CNP/GPR17+) were significantly overrepresented in intermediate- and long-term survivors (OR = 2.86, 95% CI: [2.79–2.93], Fisher’s exact p < 0.001). Validation of these findings at the protein level is ongoing using multiplex imaging (MACSima). Together, this study suggests that the spatial architecture and tumor cell state composition of H3K27M-mutant DMG may inform patient outcomes and treatment response following combination therapy with dordaviprone and paxalisib.

papers.abstract: Abstract Liquid biopsies hold promise to improve the diagnosis, assessment of response to therapy, and ultimately guide the management of cancer patients. However implementation of this approach in brain tumors has proven challenging due to the limited passage of molecules across the blood-brain barrier (BBB). In a Phase I clinical trial (NCT04528680), we transiently opened the BBB of 17 glioblastoma (GBM) patients using skull-implantable low-intensity pulsed ultrasound combined with microbubbles (LIPU/MB). Treatment and BBB opening was performed every 3 weeks with paclitaxel administration until disease progression. As an exploratory endpoint of this trial, here we investigate circulating extracellular vesicles and particles (EVPs) that get released into the circulation in the context of tumor cell death, as a potential biomarker for response to treatment. We developed and validated a microfluidic device designed to capture tumor-derived EVPs in glioblastoma patients (GlioExoChip), which leverages GBM-based expression on phosphatidylserine and Annexin-V chemistry, allowing greater than 90% capture efficiency of GBM EVPs. Proteomic analysis of circulating EVPs isolated from GBM patients revealed distinct expression patterns of SERPINA3 and APOC1 compared to healthy individuals, with tumoral origin supported by scRNA-seq analysis. A longitudinal analysis revealed concordance between EVP concentrations in plasma during LIPU/MB-based BBB disruption and MRI enhancement of tumors. Furthermore, we found changes in EVP release following the initiation of paclitaxel with LIPU/MB correlated with overall survival in GBM patients. We confirm through mechanistic in vitro experiments that paclitaxel-susceptible glioma cells exhibited apoptosis and dose-dependent EVP release. Overall, our work introduces an efficient microfluidic platform for the capture of circulating GBM EVPs that are released by glioma cells into circulation upon BBB opening following treatment-related tumor cell apoptosis. This approach represents a real-time surrogate biomarker for treatment response for a disease where imaging-based assessment of response has not been shown to be reliable.

papers.title: BIOM-67 Dynamic release of extracellular vesicles and particles after opening of the blood-brain barrier predicts glioblastoma susceptibility to paclitaxel

papers.abstract: Abstract IDH-inhibitors (IDHi) mark the first targeted therapy for IDH-mutant (IDHm) low grade gliomas (LGG). IDHis have demonstrated progression-free survival benefit, but the specific mechanisms by which patients progress while on prolonged treatment with IDHis, indicating the development of resistance, remains unknown. Our study utilizes a prospective lineage tracing technology, Cas9D10A and paired-gRNA targetable unique reporter (CAPTURE) single-cell barcoding, in five IDHm patient-derived cell line models, three oligodendroglioma and two astrocytoma, to investigate clonal dynamic responses to prolonged IDHi treatment and identify specific clonal genetic and epigenetic alterations that confer resistance to IDHi therapies in human IDHm gliomas. We observe the clonal barcode diversity between treatment and control groups to differentiate between clonal selection and individual cell plasticity. Upon identification of expanded clonal populations of interest, we proceed with live cell isolation through dual-gRNA-directed Cas9 nickase activity and subsequent Fluorescence-Activated Cell Sorting (FACS). These clonal populations are harvested for downstream applications, including bulk RNA sequencing and methylation profiling. Results thus far from GSEA analysis of bulk RNA-sequencing data indicate that short-term IDHi-treated samples with a high baseline level of the glioma’s neomorphic oncometabolite, D-2-hydroxyglutarate (D-2HG), are associated with a more mesenchymal-like phenotype over a proneural-like phenotype. More interestingly, samples with high baseline D-2HG levels develop differential upregulation of fundamental regulatory transcription factor networks when treated with an IDH-inhibitor, which correlates with the demethylation of their respective transcription factor promoters. Results from lineage tracing are validated against human IDHm glioma tissue samples that have exhibited progression while on treatment with IDHis. Our study furthers the understanding of IDHi resistance in patients with IDHm glioma, with the ultimate goals of developing combinatorial therapies to combat resistance, identifying methods to prevent resistance before it arises, and clarifying patient stratification paradigms to determine ideal candidates for IDHis.

papers.abstract: Abstract Effective therapy selection in glioblastoma (GBM) remains limited by the lack of reliable predictive biomarkers, despite advances in genomic and molecular profiling. Functional approaches that directly measure tumor drug sensitivity directly in patients and within the native tumor microenvironment may overcome these limitations. We conducted a prospective, multi-institutional Phase 1 clinical study in 12 patients with gliomas using an intratumoral drug-releasing microdevice platform adapted for prolonged implantation, which enables sustained and concomitant intratumoral exposure to diverse anticancer agents simultaneously in each patient. Drug responses were assessed in situ using multiplex immunohistochemistry as well as spatial transcriptomic profiling. Patients were followed clinically to assess progression-free survival and overall survival metrics while on systemic therapy. Prolonged intratumoral drug exposure was safe and feasible. In patients who were treated systemically with a drug which was also tested in the IMD, we observed high concordance between IMD tissue responses and clinical-radiological responses, superior to the current gold standard MGMT promoter methylation in the case of TMZ. Spatial transcriptomic analysis revealed that effective responses were associated with activation of specific pathways, including p53 signaling, apoptosis, and unfolded protein response. In contrast, resistance was associated with enrichment of broader inflammatory and survival signaling pathways, including IL6–JAK–STAT3, NF-κB, and WNT pathways. Notably, interferon-γ response was distinguished from these inflammatory programs and was enriched in regions with higher apoptotic response, suggesting a role in productive immune engagement or damage-associated signaling. Multiplex imaging demonstrated treatment-specific remodeling of the tumor immune microenvironment, including differential activation of T cell and macrophage populations. This platform offers a scalable and clinically integrable approach for elucidating intratumor mechanisms of treatment response and resistance in GBM, and to guide effective therapeutic selection.

papers.abstract: Abstract Glioblastoma (GBM) is characterized by extensive tumor heterogeneity and an immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment dominated by tumor-associated macrophages. This study investigated the prognostic and immunological significance of N-acetylneuraminate synthase (NANS), focusing on NANS-high bone marrow-derived macrophages (BMDMs). Bulk transcriptomic datasets from TCGA-GBM and CGGA cohorts were used to evaluate the prognostic relevance of NANS. Single-cell RNA-seq analysis was performed to characterize major GBM cell populations, define macrophage compartments, and examine NANS expression in microglia-derived TAMs and BMDMs. Differential expression, GO enrichment, CellChat analysis, and TCGA validation were used to define the biological and communication features of NANS-high macrophages. NANS was identified as a prognosis-associated gene, and higher NANS expression was associated with worse overall survival in TCGA-GBM. Single-cell analysis showed that NANS-positive cells were enriched in BMDMs compared with MG-TAMs. GO enrichment indicated that NANS-positive macrophages were characterized by protein folding, endoplasmic reticulum stress response, proteasome-mediated catabolism, and chaperone-related processes, suggesting enhanced proteostatic and stress-response activity. CellChat analysis revealed that NANS-high BMDMs exhibited stronger outgoing communication programs, particularly involving PLAU, GALECTIN/LGALS9, CCL, CHEMERIN, VISFATIN, GAS, ncWNT, and LIGHT signaling. Key ligand–receptor interactions included PLAU–PLAUR, LGALS9–HAVCR2/CD44/PTPRC/P4HB, and CCL3/CCL4/CCL5–CCR1/CCR5. TCGA validation further supported increased immune infiltration and elevated LGALS9, PLAU, and CCL axis activity in NANS-BMDM-high tumors. These findings suggest that NANS-high BMDMs define a prognosis-associated, immune-interactive macrophage state in GBM characterized by enhanced proteostatic activation and immunoregulatory/pro-invasive communication programs.

papers.abstract: Abstract Background Coherent Raman spectroscopy enables label-free biochemical fingerprinting of live cells with subcellular resolution. We previously developed a machine learning framework capable of classifying glioma FFPE tissues using Raman spectral signatures. We hypothesized that intrinsic biochemical composition alone is sufficient to distinguish cellular identity and tumor subtype. To test this, we generated metabolic maps of diverse brain brain-derived cell types—including astrocytoma, oligodendroglioma, and glioblastoma cells—using coherent Raman spectroscopy at single-cell resolution. Methods Patient-derived brain tumor cell lines representing genetically heterogeneous backgrounds were analyzed. Raman spectral data were acquired from 286 live single cells across the two principal molecular classes, with further subdivision into two histologic subtypes within the IDH1-mutant group, astrocytoma and oligodendroglioma. Classification was performed using an XGBoost model with shallow tree depth (1–3), a 20% held-out test set, and grouped, stratified 5-fold cross-validation to control for sample-level bias. Results and Conclusions To accelerate live cell acquisition, we first developed RADAR (Raman Spectral Analysis Using Deep Learning for Artifact Removal), a method that increases imaging speed by an order of magnitude while preserving spectral integrity. The machine learning framework distinguished IDH1-mutant from IDH1–wild-type cells with a ROC–AUC of 0.78 and further discriminated IDH1-mutant astrocytoma from oligodendroglioma cells with a ROC–AUC of 0.81. Feature importance analysis demonstrated that separation between IDH1-mutant and IDH1–wild-type cells was driven primarily by Raman peaks associated with protein amide bands, total NADH, unsaturated fatty acids, and heme-related vibrational modes. Within the IDH1-mutant class, discrimination between oligodendroglioma and astrocytoma was driven by lipid-rich vesicle signatures and protein/polyamide amide bands. These findings support the feasibility of label-free, machine learning–assisted Raman profiling to resolve clinically relevant glioma subtypes at single-cell resolution. This scalable analytical framework provides a platform for investigating metabolic heterogeneity, therapeutic response, co-culture systems, and organoid models.

papers.abstract: Abstract Glioblastoma (GBM) exhibits a complex regulatory landscape that drives its cellular heterogeneity, plasticity, and therapeutic resistance—features not fully explained by genetic alterations alone. Chromatin profiling is therefore essential to uncover the epigenetic mechanisms that encode tumor cell identity, enable state transitions, and reveal potential therapeutic vulnerabilities. Here, we implement Droplet Paired-Tag (DpT) to perform simultaneous single-cell CUT&Tag and transcriptomic profiling in GBM samples with the objective to establish a multimodal framework to define epigenetic heterogeneity and its relationship to malignant cell states in GBM. IDH-wildtype tumors from primary resections were profiled using DpT alongside complementary single-cell and spatial modalities including scRNA-seq, 10X Multiome (RNA+ATAC), and whole-transcriptome Stereo-seq. We profiled over 20,000 cells and integrated transcriptional programs with five key histone modifications marking active (H3K27ac, H3K4me1, H3K4me3) and repressive (H3K27me3, H3K9me3) chromatin. Using RNA-anchored and unbiased approaches, we explored combinatorial chromatin states underlying canonical GBM cell identities and assessed coordinated regulatory programs across modalities. Active chromatin landscapes were broadly conserved across malignant cell states, and repressive chromatin—particularly Polycomb-associated domains—showed evidence of dynamic remodeling, suggesting a role for repression in shaping cell identity and plasticity. Integration with spatial transcriptomics further enabled mapping of these regulatory states within the tumor microenvironment. Together, these results establish a spatially resolved, multimodal framework of chromatin regulation in GBM and demonstrate that malignant cell states are encoded by layered chromatin architecture rather than transcription alone.

papers.abstract: Abstract Background Spatial transcriptomics maps where cells reside but cannot tell us how a cell's transcriptome would change in a different neighborhood, a question essential for understanding niche-driven biology. This is critical in glioblastoma (GBM): immune checkpoint inhibition failed in CheckMate 143 and CheckMate 498, yet focal responses within individual tumors hint that niche architecture, not tumor identity, determines immunogenicity. Methods We built MoveSTer, a graph-attention spatial model that learns how each cell's transcriptional state depends on its spatial neighborhood, and supports counterfactual in-silico transplantation of cells across microenvironments. The model was pretrained on the Allen Brain Cell Atlas MERFISH dataset (∼7 × 106 cells) and fine-tuned on a held-out cohort of 682,813 cells from 14 IDH-wildtype human GBM Xenium samples (5,001 genes). Results MoveSTer predicted single-cell expression from spatial context with per-cell-type Spearman r = 0.66–0.94 (global per-cell zero-corrected r = 0.535) while preserving cellular identity (balanced accuracy=0.73). Counterfactual transplantation across the learned niche manifold recovered two reproducible context classes governing immune signaling. Perivascular myeloid–endothelial neighborhoods showed interferon-stimulated programs and antigen-presentation machinery (HLA-A/B/C, B2M, TAP1/2, STAT1, IRF1) co-expressed with CD274/PD-L1, consistent with an inflamed but checkpoint-suppressed state. Perineuronal neighborhoods were dominated by neural-communication signaling with low inflammatory tone. Attention analyses pointed to myeloid–endothelial versus neuronal neighbors as the main contextual correlates. In-silico transplantation of the same malignant cells across niches predicted opposing induction of interferon, stress, and mesenchymal programs, suggesting that niche identity outweighs cell identity in shaping transcriptional output. In-silico CD274 upregulation in myeloid neighbors produced dose-dependent GZMB suppression in adjacent T cells (−38% at 10×; Wilcoxon p < 0.001, n = 30 neighborhoods), consistent with known checkpoint biology. Niche assignments reproduced GBM organization previously reported by Ravi et al. (Cancer Cell 2022) and Greenwald et al. (Cell 2024). Conclusions MoveSTer predicts how single cells respond transcriptionally to their spatial context, opening counterfactual interrogation of niche-driven biology and generating testable stratification hypotheses for GBM immunotherapy trials. *Co-senior authors.

papers.title: EPCO-47 A graph-attention spatial model predicts single-cell transcriptomic responses to microenvironmental context, revealing niche-conditional immune signaling in glioblastoma

papers.abstract: Abstract Background Glioblastoma is characterized by profound spatial heterogeneity and an immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment that limits effective antitumor immunity. We and others previously showed that STING is epigenetically silenced in neoplastic glioblastoma cells, suggesting that tumor-intrinsic defects in innate immune sensing may contribute to immune evasion. However, whether STING suppression also occurs within non-neoplastic immune compartments, and how this relates to spatially organized immunosuppression, remains unclear. Methods We integrated spatial transcriptomic profiling of human glioblastoma specimens with single-cell reference mapping, bulk transcriptomic deconvolution, and CellChat-based ligand–receptor inference. Using deconvoluted bulk transcriptomes, we defined two distinct immune ecotypes – a myeloid-dominant immunosuppressive ecotype and a relatively lymphoid-enriched ecotype – and projected these signatures onto spatial transcriptomic data. Spatial neighborhoods were analyzed for STING pathway activity, hypoxia, necrosis-associated programs, VEGF signaling, interferon response, and antigen presentation. Primary and post-treatment recurrent specimens were compared to identify recurrent microenvironmental states. Results Spatial analysis identified a recurrent perinecrotic immunosuppressive niche enriched for myeloid cells, hypoxia-associated programs, and dysregulated VEGF signaling. This niche was associated with the myeloid-dominant ecotype and showed relative depletion of lymphoid ecotype features. Myeloid cells within the perinecrotic niche demonstrated suppression of STING-associated innate immune programs relative to myeloid cells in other tumor regions. CellChat analysis inferred dysregulated VEGF-associated communication, while antigen-presentation/MHC-II programs were attenuated within the niche. The STING-suppressed perinecrotic niche was observed both at diagnosis and at recurrence, suggesting that it represents a persistent feature of glioblastoma spatial organization. Conclusions These results define a treatment-persistent perinecrotic immunosuppressive niche in glioblastoma characterized by hypoxia, dysregulated VEGF-associated communication, myeloid STING suppression, and enrichment of a myeloid-dominant TME ecotype. Together with neoplastic-cell STING silencing, these findings suggest that impaired innate immune activation in glioblastoma is both tumor-cell intrinsic and spatially localized within myeloid cells of the perinecrotic tumor microenvironment.

papers.abstract: Abstract Background Large quantities of clinically meaningful neuro-oncology data remain inaccessible within unstructured electronic health records (EHRs). We investigated whether large language model (LLM)-based extraction of archived clinical records could generate biologically and clinically actionable insights. Methods We assembled one of the largest deeply annotated single-centre neuro-oncology cohorts, comprising >12,000 patients treated over eight years. Following de-identification, a Claude-based LLM pipeline converted free-text radiology, operative, histopathology, and clinical records into structured longitudinal variables. These data were integrated with treatment histories, imaging, histology and for a molecularly annotated subset of 325 patients, matched bulk genomic and transcriptomic profiling with single-cell multiomics for a smaller cohort. Multimodal survival models were developed across glioblastoma and brain metastases cohorts, and treatment-associated transcriptomic effects were evaluated. Results LLMs extracted histolopathological and radiology features and treatment intent and side effects and background health with high accuracy. Based on EHRs alone, glioblastoma one-year survival was predicted with an AUC of 0.84 overall, with robust performance across surgery plus chemoradiotherapy (AUC=0.88), surgery-only (AUC=0.82), and biopsy-only cohorts (AUC=0.80). In brain metastases, two-year survival was predicted with an AUC of 0.72, with robust performance across lung, breast and melanoma primaries. Integration of transcriptomic data identified biologically relevant treatment-associated effects. Common medications are associated with glioma transcriptional states, including suppression of neuronal/synaptic programs for ACE inhibitors (p = 0.0353) and downregulation of semaphorins, associated with invasiveness, for statins (p = 0.00680). Oestrogen replacement was associated with improved survival independent of age and sex (HR = 0.68). These findings suggest routine co-medications may influence tumour biology and should be considered in interpretation of molecular datasets and therapeutic stratification. Conclusions Routine clinical variables spanning medications, treatment, radiology, and histolopathology contain latent biological signals that systematically influence molecular interpretation and can be extracted at scale using LLMs. These variables should be considered as potential biological covariates to enable improved prognostication, surveillance optimisation, and automated identification of eligible patients for future clinical trials.

papers.abstract: Abstract Pediatric high-grade glioma (pHGG) is a lethal pediatric cancer frequently driven by histone H3.3 mutations, including H3K27M and H3G34R/V. Notably, H3G34-mutant gliomas exhibit a near-universal co-occurrence with loss of ATRX, a chromatin remodeler involved in regulation of DNA secondary structures called G-quadruplexes (G4s), though the biological basis for this coupling remains unclear. To define how histone mutation and ATRX deficiency cooperatively shape glioma biology, we generated a novel panel of six isogenic murine glioma models with controlled histone mutation status (WT, G34R, or K27M) and ATRX status (WT or deficient). We integrated RNA-, ATAC-, CUT&Tag-, and single-cell RNA-sequencing to define the epigenetic and transcriptional consequences of ATRX loss in histone-mutant glioma. Bulk RNA- and ATAC-seq demonstrated that ATRX loss promotes migratory transcriptional programs while suppressing neural differentiation pathways in ATRX-deficient H3G34R murine glioma cells. CUT&Tag profiling of bivalent histone marks H3K4me3 and H3K27me3 identified ATRX-induced promoter H3K4me3 gain and H3K27me3 loss at loci linked to invasiveness and neural stemness, including FN1 and SOX1, accompanied by increased gene expression. Approximately two-thirds of genes with concordant promoter H3K4me3 gain and transcriptional upregulation contained promoter G4s, including FN1. G4 formation is enriched at H3K4me3-bound promoters, supporting a model in which unresolved G4s in an ATRX-deficient setting facilitate H3K4 methyltransferase recruitment and stemness-associated transcription. Pharmacologic stabilization of G4 structures in ATRX-intact G34R cells phenocopied ATRX loss, increasing promoter H3K4me3 binding at migratory and neural stemness genes. Single-cell RNA sequencing of isogenic G34R models suggest that H3G34R ATRX-deficient tumors suppress mature interneuronal gene programs, including GABA import and secretion, consistent with the interneuronal precursor cell-of-origin previously described in G34R glioma. Altogether, these findings reveal a mechanism by which ATRX loss cooperates with H3G34R mutation, promoting G-quadruplex–dependent dysregulation of H3K4 methyltransferase recruitment at bivalent promoters to reinforce neural stemness and migration-associated programs.

papers.abstract: Abstract Glioblastoma IDH-wildtype (GBM) tumors exhibit substantial genetic and transcriptional intra-tumoral heterogeneity. GBM transcriptional cell states are highly plastic, as they can be either stably inherited or transition between different states across cell divisions. However, cell intrinsic and extrinsic features that determine the spatial architecture, heritability and encoding of GBM cell states remains poorly understood. Existing technologies allow for profiling of transcriptionally-defined cell states along space or time, but not both, precluding analysis of how cell ancestry and cell location relate to each other in primary human tumors. Here, we develop single-cell frameworks for the analysis of primary human tumors at scale that combine (i) high-throughput lineage tracing from single cell Whole-Genome Sequencing (scWGS), (ii) cell phenotyping from matched transcriptome and (iii) macroscopic multi-regional and microscopic spatial genomics analysis that records cells’ spatial localization prior to downstream single-cell analysis. Applied to 28 multi-region samples from nine GBM patients, this multi-omics integration allowed us to construct high-resolution, phenotypically annotated single-cell phylogenies to simultaneously analyze cell ancestry, GBM cell state and spatial localization of 2106 single cells. This analysis determined the heritability and plasticity of cell states in relation to genetic events, including extrachromosomal DNA (ecDNA) presence, and tumor microenvironment (TME) features. High-resolution phylogenetic analysis tracked ecDNA evolution, uncovering dynamic remodeling of ecDNA architecture across subclones and quantifying how oncogene dosage drives transitions between differentiated and stem-like cellular states. Phylodynamic analysis of tumor regions, including the infiltrating edge, enhancing edge and necrotic core obtained from multi-regional sampling, and TME features, including immune and neuronal cell presence obtained from single nucleus barcoding, revealed cell-extrinsic features impacting GBM cell states. Collectively, this work provides a high-resolution window into GBM evolution at the genetic, cell state and spatial levels, unifying analysis across these modalities to provide insights into GBM heterogeneity, directly from patient tumors.

papers.abstract: Abstract Digital twins (DT) are emerging as a promising framework for predictive oncology; however, most current models remain largely static and poorly suited to capture the dynamic nature of tumor biology. Here, we introduce a perturbation-driven-DT framework based on the concept of a Minimum Viable Digital Twin (MV-DT): the smallest biologically meaningful and experimentally tractable system capable of iterative learning and refinement. Using oligodendroglioma as a model of highly heterogeneous gliomas, we developed a multiscale MV-DT integrating transcriptomics, tumor ecosystem modelling, molecular network analysis, and PhysiCell-based agent simulations to reconstruct tumor microenvironment (TME) dynamics. Cellular composition was reconstructed from bulk and single-cell transcriptomic datasets using MuSiC-based deconvolution, enabling quantitative estimation of TME cell populations for initialization of the agent-based glioma model. To move beyond descriptive molecular profiling, we implemented the ClauNab (Smart-Scoring-System (3S)), integrating gene expression, network topology, and functional modularity to identify biologically relevant regulatory programs associated with tumor progression. This systems-level approach identified pathological modules linked to proliferation, epigenetic regulation (UHRF1-EZH2), extracellular matrix remodeling (FN1-CD44), immune signaling, and inflammatory pathways such as CXCL12–CXCR4 and JAK-STAT. Intercellular communication networks reconstructed using CellChat revealed ECM-centered signaling hubs and immune-modulatory axes coordinating tumor spatial organization and progression. These molecular and cellular layers were integrated into a unified PhysiCell-based DT capable of reproducing key neuropathological features of glioma biology, including spatial heterogeneity and TME gradients. In parallel, AI-driven drug discovery using the BIOVIA platform identified promising FDA-approved compounds targeting UHRF1 and EZH2 with predicted target specificity, blood–brain-barrier permeability, and low toxicity profiles. These candidates provided a rational basis for PhysiCell inhibition simulations to investigate the inhibition impact on cancer stem cell survival and TME dynamics. Together, this work redefines glioma DT as adaptive learning systems providing a scalable framework for biomarker discovery, therapeutic response prediction, and precision neuro-oncology.

papers.abstract: Abstract Medulloblastoma (MB) is a highly malignant pediatric cerebellar tumor comprising molecularly and clinically distinct subgroups. Group 3 and Group 4 MBs are believed to arise from overlapping progenitor populations within the developing rhombic lip (RL), when neuronal differentiation is stalled secondary to somatic driver events. Genetic alterations predicted to perturb transcription factor (TF) activity are pervasive in Groups 3 and 4 MB, suggesting that dysregulated gene regulatory programs drive MB pathogenesis. However, tumor-specific transcriptional signatures provoking and sustaining tumorigenesis remain poorly understood. Herein, we leveraged single-cell multiome datasets of MB and the developing human cerebellum to resolve gene expression programs and associated TF activity underlying malignancy in Groups 3 and 4 MB. Comparative analysis of MB transcriptomes and accessible chromatin landscapes with their cerebellar counterparts in the developing RL revealed profound disruption of neurogenic transcriptional networks, including master TFs such as OTX2 and NFIB. Genome-wide in vitro CRISPR screens further indicated that many of these TFs represent MB-selective growth dependencies. CRISPR-mediated inhibition and targeted protein degradation validated prioritized TFs as strong dependencies in Group 3 MB cell lines in vitro. Ongoing studies are focused on evaluating dysregulated transcriptional circuitry as a tumor-maintenance vulnerability in physiologically relevant contexts through in vivo CRISPR screens in Group 3 and Group 4 MB patient-derived xenograft models and investigating the molecular mechanisms governing TF dysregulation and dependency. Together, these studies aim to uncover actionable transcriptional vulnerabilities and provide a foundation for the development of mechanism-driven targeted therapies for high-risk MB subgroups.

papers.abstract: Abstract Pediatric-type diffuse high-grade gliomas (pHGGs) are aggressive central nervous system tumors that are the leading cause of cancer-related death in children. pHGGs comprise histologically, genetically, and molecularly distinct subtypes with characteristic driver mutations, anatomical localizations, and ages of onset. Although pHGGs share many features with adult gliomas, they represent clinically and biologically distinct tumor entities. Despite growing insights into the cellular architectures of pHGGs, the evolution of malignant cell states and tumor microenvironments during tumor progression remains largely unexplored. In this study, we generated an extensive longitudinal single-nucleus and spatial transcriptomic atlas of pediatric high-grade gliomas (pHGG) from children, adolescents and young adults using single-nucleus RNA sequencing and Xenium In Situ spatial transcriptomics. Our cohort includes 49 paired HGG samples across tumor subtypes, spanning diffuse midline glioma (DMG), IDH-mutant (IDH-HGG) and H3-and IDH-wildtype high-grade glioma (HGG), representing the most comprehensive longitudinal pediatric glioma cohort profiled to date. Single-nucleus profiling uncovered shared and distinct cellular subpopulations in different pHGG subtypes. Despite notable similarities in transcriptional profiles of primary and recurrent pHGGs, recurrent HGGs showed increased proportions of malignant cells with a hypoxia-associated program, coupled with a reduction in malignant glial-like cell populations. Spatial transcriptomic analysis of 71 tumor sections from 31 pHGGs revealed subtype-specific global spatial organizations and localized cellular niches. Upon analyzing the density of tissue regions, we found that the normal cells occur in less dense regions than malignant cells; within the malignant compartments, we found OPC-like cells consistently existed in denser regions than AC-like cells. Overall, our study characterizes the cellular landscape and spatial architecture across pHGG subtypes and provides a detailed delineation of the spatiotemporal dynamics during progression, paving the way for the identification of novel therapeutic targets.

papers.abstract: Abstract Gliomas are aggressive brain tumors with poor prognosis and limited response to immunotherapy, largely due to an immunologically inert tumor microenvironment. Oncolytic virotherapy, such as the engineered herpesvirus G207, has shown promise in early phase clinical trials in recurrent high-grade gliomas by turning “cold” tumors to “hot”, yet the spatial and cellular mechanisms underlying these effects remain poorly understood. Here, we combine spatially resolved transcriptomics and single-nucleus RNA sequencing of nearly 5 million cells from 34 patient samples to profile tumors before and after G207 treatment, revealing the emergence of a unique immune-vascular niche, which we term Naïve T cell Organizing Vascular Assembly (NOVA). These NOVAs are enriched for naive CD8+ T cells, supported by a vascular-immune mixed compartment, and exhibit reduced apoptotic and cytotoxic signaling. Ligand-receptor and transcriptional analyses highlight crosstalk between vascular and immune cells, promoting T cell persistence and stem-like traits. Comparative analyses with other virotherapies, immunotherapy and standard of care treatments confirm that NOVAs are a distinct oHSV post-treatment phenomenon. These structures differ from previously described tertiary lymphoid structures or perivascular niches, representing a novel lymphoid-like niche associated with long-term survival. Our findings delineate the molecular and cellular architecture of NOVAs, offering mechanistic insight into anti-tumor immunity and providing a framework to guide rational design of immunovirotherapy strategies in malignant brain tumors.

papers.abstract: Abstract Background Atypical teratoid rhabdoid tumors (ATRT) are aggressive central nervous system malignancies that typically occur before three years of age. Current multi-modal therapies lead to severe treatment-related toxicities, necessitating improved therapeutic strategies. Here we propose Heat Shock Protein 90 (HSP90) as a target in ATRT. HSP90 stabilizes client oncoproteins in cancer cells, and HSP90 inhibitors (HSP90i) are well-tolerated in clinical trials. Heat Shock Protein 90 Alpha Family Class A Member 1 (HSP90AA1) encodes the stress-inducible isoform of HSP90. Methods We utilized publicly available data from patient-derived ATRT cells to identify potential vulnerabilities in vitro. Comparisons were performed between 20 ATRT and 39 non-malignant cell lines across RNA-sequencing and pharmacologic screens to identify selective dependencies in ATRT. Genome-wide CRISPR-Cas9 depletion screens across five ATRT cell lines were further analyzed to detect vulnerabilities. Candidate validation is underway, harnessing CRISPR-Cas9 genetic knockout coupled with drug, cell viability, and neurosphere formation assays. Results Out of 1,807 drugs tested, 24 yielded significantly lower Z-scores (FDR < 0.05) in ATRT cells relative to non-malignant cells. Despite HSP90i constituting < 0.01% of the drug panel, 20% of these 24 compounds were HSP90i. The average Z-score across all six HSP90i was -2.62 for ATRT and -0.83 for non-malignant cells. Additionally, HSP90AA1 was a genetic dependency (FDR < 0.05, Z < -3) in ATRT. HSP90AA1 was also significantly overexpressed (FDR < 0.05) in ATRT relative to non-malignant cells and highly expressed in ATRT compared to other pediatric cancers. Using CellTiter-Glo to assess cell viability, we determined the half maximal inhibitory concentrations (IC50) of the blood-brain-barrier-penetrant HSP90i onalespib to be 39.50, 104.1, and 27.91 nM in CHLA-05-ATRT, CHLA-06-ATRT, and BT-16, respectively. Ongoing experiments will evaluate HSP90i in combination with cytotoxic chemotherapy and identify client proteins in ATRT using mass spectrometry. Conclusion HSP90 inhibition is a promising therapeutic strategy in ATRT.
