papers.abstract: Abstract Leptomeningeal dissemination of high-grade glioma is a rare but devastating complication with no established standard of care. The intrathecal compartment is anatomically suited to locoregional therapy, yet no agent has been rationally matched to glioma biology in this setting. Here, we used functional genomic screening and drug-target network integration in patient-derived glioma models to identify and validate a genetically stratified vulnerability. Analysis of a proprietary large-scale CRISPRi screen in primary patient-derived glioma tumour spheres identified DNA replication and polymerase-linked pathways as dominant liabilities. Network-based integration of these dependencies with pathway annotations, molecular interaction networks, and drug-target relationships nominated cytarabine as a clinically available agent targeting this vulnerability. Cytarabine is a nucleoside analogue with established intrathecal clinical use, including in leptomeningeal disease, but its rational deployment in glioma has remained largely empirical. We profiled cytarabine dose-response across molecularly diverse patient-derived glioma tumour sphere models and observed a > 200-fold range in (IC50 » 0.04–9.8 µM). Machine-learning analysis of whole-genome sequencing-derived features identified TP53, RB1 and no chromosome 10q (chr10q) loss as dominant predictors of response. Patient samples with TP53/RB1 wild-type genotype and no chr10q loss showed markedly increased cytarabine sensitivity compared with TP53- and/or RB1-altered models or chr10q loss genotype. Ongoing single-cell profiling of cytarabine-treated mixed GBM tumour spheres (n = 51) is testing whether this genotype-response relationship is preserved within heterogeneous tumour groups and is designed to resolve clonal and transcriptional features associated with cytarabine sensitivity. Together, these findings identify cytarabine as a mechanistically anchored, biomarker-stratified repurposing opportunity in glioma, with TP53/RB1 wild-type and chr10q copy number neutral status nominating a molecular subgroup with enhanced sensitivity. Given cytarabine’s existing clinical use in the intrathecal setting, these data support further evaluation of genetic biomarker-guided administration of cytarabine for leptomeningeal glioma, extending bulk viability biomarkers into single-cell, heterogeneity-aware therapeutic stratification.

papers.title: EPCO-12 Functional genomics nominates cytarabine as a biomarker-guided therapy for leptomeningeal glioma

papers.abstract: Abstract Alternative splicing derived neoantigens can be served as promising immunotherapeutic targets for tumor. However, little is known about the AS milieu in Pediatric brain tumor, including diffuse midline glioma (DMG), ependymoma (EPN), atypical teratoid/rhabdoid tumor (ATRT), meningioma (MG), dysembryoplastic neuroepithelial tumor (DNET), craniopharyngioma (CPG), choroid plexus papilloma (CPP), neurofibromatosis (NF), primitive neuroectodermal tumours (PNET), Schwannomas(SCH), pediatric low-grade glioma(pLGG), pediatric high grade glioma (pHGG) and medulloblastoma (MB). We performed integrated analysis of alternative splicing using bulk RNA-seq and single cell RNA-seq datasets of 1,000 pediatric brain tumor specimens across 15 cancer types, including 90 DMG, 25 EPN, 90 ATRT, 73 CPG, 23 CPP, 38 DNET, 40 MG, 29 NF, 24 PNET, 30 SCH, 30 MG, 409 pLGG, 45 pHGG, 50 MB and 190 EPN cases. We also re-analyzed RNA-sequencing data from non-malignant human brain tissues. We reconstructed the landscape of AS in Pediatric glioma and contrasted that to observed isoforms in non-malignant brain. We found that AS score can be used to stratify the MB patients samples, and high AS score was significantly associated with worse survival in MB. We identified novel splicing events in cell-surface proteins that are suitable targets for engineered T-cell therapies in these 15 cancer types. We also identified novel splicing events derived neoantigens in DMG, EPN, ATRT, CPG, CPP, DNET, MG, NF, PNET, SCH, MG, pLGG, pHGG, MB and EPN respectively, which are potential immunotherapy targets. We found MB specific isoforms of transforming growth factor beta (TGFβ) signaling pathway genes which are expressed exclusively by MB tumor cells. Our studies shed light on the effect of immunotherapy on AS and identify novel targets for emerging immunotherapies in pediatric brain tumor.

papers.abstract: Abstract Glioblastoma recurrence timing and mechanisms remain difficult to predict, limiting risk-adapted surveillance and therapy. We developed a scalable, biologically interpretable framework to predict continuous time to recurrence (TTR) from H&E histopathology, using spatial molecular profiling to define recurrence-associated biology underlying model predictions without requiring advanced assays for deployment. Tumors from 40 patients (n = 80 specimens) with documented TTR and multimodal profiling underwent Xenium spatial transcriptomics, CODEX multiplexed proteomic imaging, H&E analysis, preoperative MRI analysis, and clinical annotation. Xenium data were processed in Seurat and annotated into astrocyte-like, oligodendrocyte progenitor-like, neural progenitor-like, mesenchymal-like, and proliferative malignant programs. Spatial architecture was quantified by k-means clustering of local cell-type composition, defining 12 niches. CODEX was integrated with Xenium using MaxFuse to refine immune subtype resolution. H&E slides were annotated for necrosis, infiltrating tumor, and tumor core; whole-slide images were tiled with SlideFlow, and UNI-derived tile embeddings were used to fine-tune a model identifying TTR-associated regions. High-attention regions were mapped to spatial gene-expression programs and histopathologic annotations. Preoperative MRI features were analyzed with PyRadiomics and integrated where available. Spatial analyses identified architectures varying along the TTR continuum. Shorter-TTR tumors showed malignant-cell infiltration across niches, disrupting immune and stromal organization. Longer-TTR tumors retained compartmentalized vascular-, immune-, and endothelial-rich regions, supported by H&E review. Shorter-TTR tumors were enriched for undifferentiated neural progenitor-like cells, up to ∼52% of malignant cells, and proliferative states, up to ∼14%. Longer-TTR tumors showed higher differentiated astrocyte-like, mesenchymal-like, and oligodendrocyte progenitor-like programs, often >60% combined, with lower proliferation, <10%. An oligodendrocyte-enriched niche showed greater lymphoid localization in longer-TTR tumors (Wilcoxon adjusted P = 0.0037), supporting association between TTR and spatial immune compartmentalization. These findings suggest that routine H&E contains recurrence-relevant morphologic information. Linking deployable histopathology to differentiation state, proliferative burden, radiographic features, and tumor–immune–vascular organization supports recurrence-risk modeling and biologically grounded patient stratification.

papers.abstract: Abstract Glioblastoma (GBM) is a lethal brain cancer with poor clinical outcomes. Although immunotherapies such as immune checkpoint blockade and CAR-T cells have shown promise in other cancers, they have had limited efficacy in GBM clinical trials. One major barrier is the profound heterogeneity of GBM, which includes mesenchymal-like (MES), astrocyte-like (AC), oligodendrocyte-progenitor-like (OPC), and neural-progenitor-like (NPC) states that may engage distinct mechanisms of immunosuppression. However, reliable immunocompetent mouse models that recapitulate GBM subtype heterogeneity remain limited. To address this gap, we engineered murine neural crest stem cell lines carrying common GBM-associated alterations, including EgfrvIII to model AC-like tumors, PdgfraN659K to model OPC-like tumors, and Nf1-/-;Trp53-/- to model MES-like tumors. Single-cell RNA sequencing revealed that PdgfraN659K tumors were enriched for OPC-like states, whereas EgfrvIII and Nf1-/-;Trp53-/- tumors showed stronger AC- and MES-like programs, suggesting distinct modes of GBM heterogeneity. Analysis of tumor-infiltrating immune cells further revealed subtype-specific immune landscapes. PdgfraN659K tumors showed increased microglial infiltration, EgfrvIII tumors were enriched for immunosuppressive tumor-associated macrophages, and Nf1-/-;Trp53-/- tumors contained higher numbers of T and B cells. Importantly, gene signatures distinguishing these murine models mapped differentially onto human glioma single-cell RNA-seq datasets, indicating that these models capture key aspects of human GBM heterogeneity. Using Xenium spatial single-cell profiling, we further found that EgfrvIII tumors exhibited elevated extracellular matrix (ECM) gene expression and markedly reduced T- and B-cell infiltration compared with Nf1-/-;Trp53-/- tumors. In parallel, our group has shown that BRD2 promotes MES-like GBM programs, and pharmacologic BRD2 inhibition reduces ECM gene expression in patient-derived GBM cell lines. Combining BRD2 inhibition with anti-PD-1 immune checkpoint blockade prolonged survival compared with anti-PD-1 alone in the MES-enriched 005 murine model. By integrating single-cell, spatial transcriptomic, and therapeutic perturbation approaches, this work provides mechanistic insight into GBM immunosuppression and identifies potential strategies to improve immunotherapy responses.

papers.abstract: Abstract Diffuse intrinsic pontine glioma (DIPG) is a leading cause of cancer-related death in children, with no curative therapy. GD2-CAR T cell therapy has shown promising results in early clinical trials, but responses are variable and nearly all patients relapse. The brainstem location, intratumoral heterogeneity, and tumor-supportive microenvironment make DIPG uniquely difficult to treat, and how the microenvironment differs in patients exposed to immunotherapy remains poorly characterized. Single-cell resolution spatial transcriptomics now enables study of tumor cell states and cell-cell interactions in their spatial context, offering an opportunity to identify drivers of progression and therapy resistance. Here, we present the first spatial atlas of GD2-CAR treated DIPG, generated on the Xenium Prime platform from an autopsy cohort of ten patients treated with GD2-CAR T cell therapy and nine without immunotherapy, with matched single-nucleus RNA sequencing. The dataset comprises over 3 million high-quality cells profiled across more than 5,000 genes, exceeding prior single-cell transcriptomic cohorts of H3K27M-mutant gliomas by more than an order of magnitude. This scale and spatial resolution enables statistically powered niche and cell-cell interaction analyses that smaller datasets cannot support. A major challenge in DIPG is distinguishing malignant from non-malignant cells given their overlapping expression profiles. We addressed this by performing post-Xenium immunofluorescence for the H3K27M mutation on the same tissue sections, allowing direct identification of malignant cells in situ. H3K27M-defined malignant clusters were concordant with malignant signatures derived from matched snRNA-seq, and we further derived a spatial malignant signature from H3K27M-positive cells. GD2-CAR T cells were detected directly using a custom Xenium probe. Spatial autocorrelation analysis identified co-varying gene modules organized into distinct tissue niches, including modules enriched for neuron-glia signaling and myeloid regulatory programs. This high-resolution map of the DIPG microenvironment will nominate candidate cell-cell interactions for functional testing in preclinical models, informing future combination strategies for GD2-CAR T cell therapy.

papers.abstract: Abstract Cancer immunotherapy is relatively ineffective in glioblastoma (GBM). This therapeutic failure can be attributed to tissue and cellular heterogeneity, a predominantly pro-tumor immune microenvironment, and tumor cell-intrinsic immune evasive and suppressive mechanisms. Characterization of spatially distinct immunosuppressive cell types and the mechanisms they employ to modulate the anti-tumor immune response represents a promising avenue for targeted therapeutics. We leveraged the high-resolution capabilities of Xenium spatial transcriptomics, alongside single-cell RNA-sequencing, to dissect niche-specific cellular compositions and phenotypes in patient GBMs. Samples were obtained from patients in a clinical trial for oncolytic virus treatment and include both pre- and post-virus tumor tissue. Computational-based neighborhood analysis revealed diverse tissue patterning and differential infiltration of various immune cell types. Specifically, T cells were significantly enriched in samples post-oncolytic virus, but poorly infiltrated hypoxic tumor regions. Notably, T cells in the hypoxic niche had altered expression of functional programs and were especially enriched for Killer Cell Lectin-Like Receptor B1 (KLRB1) expression. Importantly, CLEC2D (LLT1), which binds KLRB1-encoded CD161, was uniquely upregulated in Mes2-like tumor cells, a hypoxic subset of mesenchymal GBM cells, and co-localized with KLRB1 expression. Of note, CD161-LLT1 interaction is a known mechanism of suppressing effector T cell function. Furthermore, CLEC2D and several factors involved in immune cell recruitment were more highly expressed in post-virus samples. These data demonstrate a novel hypoxic context for tumor cell-mediated immune regulation afforded by the unique degree of immune infiltration in response to immunotherapy. Future investigation will explore the in vivo consequences of CD161-LLT1 interaction in the hypoxic niche in an effort to elucidate T cell-suppressing tumor cell function.

papers.abstract: Abstract Introduction Leptomeningeal disease (LMD) is a late-stage, devastating neurological complication of multiple solid tumors, including GBM, in which tumor cells attach to the arachnoid and pial membranes that form the leptomeninges. A unifying feature of these cells is their ability to survive without substrate anchorage, in the nutrient-poor, hypoxic, acidic milieu of CSF. We hypothesized, therefore, that an ex vivo model system that selects for anchorage-independent clonogenic tumor growth may yield cancer cells adapted for LMD when injected directly into the CSF. Methods Using a novel microwell clonogenic device (10K microwells/1 cm2 chamber x 4 chambers per device (SingleCell Biotechnology) treated to create an ultralow-adhesion (ULA) surface, we tracked the fate of thousands of microwells each containing a single cell over a period of 7 days using a custom deep machine learning image analysis pipeline. Multiple cancer subtypes were assessed. Results A minor population of U251 GBM cells adapted to the ULA state was able to form multicellular clones in the microwells at 7 days. Direct intra-cisternal injection of these cells produced lethal LMD in all mice in 3 weeks (n = 9), while mice injected with parental cells remained asymptomatic for up to 8 weeks. Multi-omic analysis of parental and U251-ULA- adapted cells displayed chromosomal-level changes, stress-associated transcription factor upregulation, anti-ROS mechanisms, and activation of ECM signaling pathways. Similar changes in integrin signaling were observed in multiple ULA-adapted cancer cell lines derived from both CNS and non-CNS tumors. CRISPR deletion of integrin receptors (α6, β1) in glioma cells resulted in a marked reduction of LMD but did not impact tumor growth when the same cells were injected directly into the brain parenchyma. Conclusion These data provide mechanistic insights into the adaptive changes that tumor cells must undergo to develop LMD and suggests a commonality among cancer subtypes.

papers.abstract: Abstract Background Glioblastoma (GBM) remains a universally lethal disease, defined by extensive intratumoral heterogeneity, dynamic cell state plasticity, and a profoundly immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment. These features have collectively constrained the efficacy of adoptive cellular immunotherapies. A central unmet need is the identification of surface antigens exhibiting broad expression across GBM cell states with a favorable safety profile relative to normal CNS tissue. Methods We constructed a single-nucleus RNA sequencing atlas integrating GBM patient specimens, normal adult brain, and developmental brain references, and applied machine learning to systematically prioritize surface antigens based on on-tumor expression breadth and off-tumor liability, nominating PTPRZ1 as a high-priority candidate with near-ubiquitous expression across GBM transcriptional states and a favorable therapeutic index. To generate functional binding agents, we pursued parallel discovery campaigns producing scFv and single-domain nanobody repertoires via murine and camelid immunization, respectively. Both libraries underwent phage display with iterative cell-based selection against native PTPRZ1 at physiologically relevant tumor-surface densities — directly addressing the critical limitation of previously described binding agents, which fail to recognize PTPRZ1 at endogenous tumor levels — with stringent counter-selection against closely related phosphatase family members to ensure specificity. Lead candidates from both modalities were subjected to directed evolution through protein language model-guided affinity maturation, converging on a unique PTPRZ1 epitope accessible at physiological expression levels. Optimized binding domains were incorporated into CAR constructs with engineered co-stimulatory architectures designed to maximize sensitivity under low antigen-density conditions. Results PTPRZ1-directed CAR T cells demonstrated robust cytotoxicity against patient-derived GBM stem-like cell cultures in vitro and significant tumor burden reduction in orthotopic xenograft models in vivo, outperforming constructs based on previously described binding agents. Conclusions We report the discovery of PTPRZ1 as a GBM surface antigen and a complete engineering pipeline — from single-cell antigen nomination to epitope-focused directed evolution — that resolves the physiological recognition barrier limiting prior approaches, establishing a translational rationale for PTPRZ1-directed CAR T cell therapy.

papers.abstract: Abstract Antiproliferative therapies can induce cellular senescence, a state characterized by stable cell-cycle arrest and acquisition of a senescence-associated secretory phenotype (SASP). SASP factors released from senescent cells can further propagate senescence to neighboring cells through paracrine signaling. In our previously published phase-1b clinical trial of intracranial topotecan delivered by convection-enhanced delivery (CED) in recurrent glioblastoma, immunostaining of post-treatment biopsies demonstrated an elevation of the senescence marker p21. Gene set enrichment analysis (GSEA) of bulk RNA sequencing data showed post-treatment enrichment of the SaulSenMayo senescence gene signature. Subsequent CIBERSORT deconvolution revealed this enrichment was specific to myeloid cells. To model therapy-induced senescence, TS543 glioma cells were treated with escalating concentrations of topotecan, and senescence induction was validated by morphologic assessment, immunocytochemical staining, and bulk RNA sequencing for established senescence-associated pathways. Conditioned media collected from senescent glioma cultures was subsequently applied to HMC3 microglia and iPSC-derived microglia. In parallel, microglia were treated directly with topotecan. Senescence in recipient microglia was evaluated by immunocytochemistry, qPCR, EdU incorporation assays, and bulk RNA sequencing. Additionally, mice underwent seven days of intracranial topotecan administration by CED followed by single-cell RNA sequencing analysis. Both conditioned media from senescent glioma cells and direct topotecan exposure induced senescence-associated phenotypes in microglia. Microglia demonstrated increased p21 and p16 expression, reduced EdU incorporation, and enrichment of senescence-associated transcriptional programs, including the SaulSenMayo gene set. In the murine CED model, topotecan treatment similarly induced senescence pathway enrichment in both tumor and microglial populations at seven days. Together, these findings demonstrate that topotecan-induced senescence extends beyond tumor cells and propagates to tumor-associated microglia through both direct and paracrine mechanisms. These results suggest that SASP-mediated secondary senescence may contribute to persistence of a therapy-altered, potentially treatment-resistant tumor microenvironment following chemotherapy exposure.

papers.abstract: Abstract Meningioma is the most common primary intracranial tumor in adults. Although often benign, malignant meningiomas remain difficult to treat due to poor responses to surgery and radiotherapy. Immunotherapy has improved outcomes across many cancers but has shown limited efficacy in malignant meningiomas, partly due to exclusion of T cells from the tumor microenvironment (TME), resulting in an immunologically “cold” tumor phenotype. Recently, our team identified phospholipase A2 group 10 (PLA2G10) as a key factor contributing to T cell exclusion. PLA2G10 is highly expressed in several human cancers, where it suppresses T cell infiltration and reduces responsiveness to anti–PD-1 therapy. These findings suggest that targeting PLA2G10 may enhance immunotherapy efficacy in malignant meningiomas. Single-cell RNA sequencing analysis of publicly available datasets identified distinct cell clusters expressing PLA2G10 and characterized immune-related gene expression patterns, supporting its role in modulating the meningioma TME. Multispectral Multiplex Immunofluorescence imaging of meningioma tissue microarray samples demonstrated PLA2G10 expression in over 50% of cases across all tumor grades. Investigation of the IOMM-LEE meningioma cell line further demonstrated secretion of PLA2G10, suggesting a functional role in shaping the tumor microenvironment. To evaluate the therapeutic potential of PLA2G10 targeting, an IOMM-LEE cell line with PLA2G10 CRISPR knockout was generated and heterotopically injected into the subcutaneous flank of NSG mice alongside a control cell line with intact PLA2G10 expression. Both groups received CAR-T cells targeting B7-H3. Mice implanted with PLA2G10 CRISPR knockout IOMM-LEE cells demonstrated significantly improved tumor control following treatment with CAR-T cells targeting B7-H3 compared with control tumors. PLA2G10 is a novel immunotherapy target that contributes to T cell exclusion in meningiomas. Targeting PLA2G10 may enhance T cell infiltration and improve CAR-T therapy efficacy. Further studies investigating cell type-specific PLA2G10 expression and biomarker-driven patient selection may guide future clinical trial design and optimize therapeutic responses.

papers.abstract: Abstract Immunotherapy increases survival in mouse glioma models, but this is not observed in clinical trials. To address the differences between human and mouse gut microbiota, we employed a humanized microbiome (HuM) mouse model by transplanting fecal matter from healthy human donors into gnotobiotic mice. In the GL261 glioma model, HuM mouse lines could be classified as either responders or nonresponders to anti-PD-1 therapy. Here, we investigated the immune differences between these HuM lines in naïve and glioma conditions. Single-cell RNA sequencing of naïve colonic CD45+ cells revealed that responder colons had higher neutrophil and B cell frequencies, increased Tlr2 expression, increased Il17a/f expression in effector cells, elevated trafficking markers, and an increase in predicted oxidative phosphorylation. Using flow cytometry, the gut and brain-draining LNs of responders had a higher frequency of Rorγt+ CD4+ T cells than nonresponders. The observed Tlr2 expression and Th17 response suggest that lipoteichoic acid (LTA) from gram-positive bacteria may enhance therapy response, consistent with the higher abundance of gram-positive bacteria in the responder fecal samples. To directly test causality, our ongoing studies are evaluating whether oral LTA supplementation can convert nonresponders to responders, and whether TLR2 blockade abrogates therapeutic benefit of anti-PD-1 in responder lines in the murine model of glioma. These experiments are designed to establish a mechanistic link between microbiota-derived ligands and anti-PD-1 efficacy. In total, this work highlights a microbiota-TLR2-Th17 axis that may underlie differential anti-PD-1 immunotherapy responses and could be a targetable pathway to improve glioma outcomes.

papers.abstract: Abstract Recurrent malignant gliomas are resistant to conventional treatments. These tumors exhibit a paucity of tumor-infiltrating lymphocytes (TILs) and a characteristically low immunogenic profile. Delta-24-RGD, an oncolytic adenovirus engineered to selectively replicate in cancer cells, has demonstrated a favorable safety profile and objective clinical responses in several pediatric and adult glioma trials. In addition, Delta-24-RGD treatment transforms the immunologically “cold” tumor microenvironment into a more immunologically active, or “hot,” state, providing a unique opportunity to analyze TCR repertoires and anti-tumoral TIL-associated signatures. In this study, we performed T cell receptor (TCR) sequencing and spatial transcriptomics analyses on tumors from a window-of-opportunity clinical trial of Delta-24-RGD in malignant gliomas. We showed that virotherapy profoundly reshapes the intratumoral TCR repertoire, with only 20% of TCRs shared between pre- and post-treatment samples. Virotherapy also significantly reduced TCR diversity (p = 0.036), and notably, post-treatment TCR diversity was positively correlated with patient survival (p = 0.022). Spatial transcriptomics using the Xenium platform identified specific immune programs that correlated with therapy response (p = 0.0067). In conclusion, this study provides a comprehensive analysis of immune cell populations in gliomas treated with oncolytic adenoviruses and demonstrates that oncolytic virotherapy markedly alters the immune landscape in recurrent gliomas, and that specific immune features may serve as biomarkers of therapeutic response.

papers.abstract: Abstract Glioblastoma resists immunotherapy through immunosuppression, limited T-cell infiltration, and spatial immune exclusion. GIANT (NCT06816927) tests whether perioperative PD-1/LAG-3 blockade remodels local tumor microenvironment (TME) and systemic immunity. Patients undergo biopsy, nivolumab plus relatlimab 8–14 days before resection, then postoperative therapy, with longitudinal tumor, CSF, PBMC, microbiome, imaging, and outcome assessment. Primary endpoints are feasibility and tumor-infiltrating lymphocyte density in paired pre- and post-treatment tumors. Stage 1 is a safety and biologic-activity run-in of 6–12 patients, including ≥6 MGMT-methylated patients, to establish safety with radiotherapy, temozolomide, nivolumab, and relatlimab. Stage 2 will randomize 80 patients preoperatively 1:3 to nivolumab versus nivolumab plus relatlimab to isolate LAG-3 contribution, followed by postoperative nivolumab plus relatlimab; MGMT-unmethylated patients omit temozolomide. Each patient undergoes 10 MRI-guided, spatially annotated biopsies before resection, profiled by flow cytometry, IHC, Xenium 5100-gene spatial transcriptomics, and CODEX proteomics. Biopsies are spatially registered to reconstruct 3D tumor architecture and define molecular, cellular, and histologic heterogeneity. From January–May 2026, four patients enrolled in Stage 1: two males, median age 64.5 years, ECOG 0–1, and two MGMT-methylated. Perioperative therapy was feasible; inflammatory edema occurred in two patients, one requiring expedited surgery, with full recovery. Despite heterogeneous radiographic tumor enlargement/cavitation, post-treatment flow cytometry showed marked CD45+ immune infiltration in evaluable tumors, comprising 33%, 87%, and 50% of cells in three patients. In one tumor, T cells ranged from 5% centrally to 30% at the edge, showing regional immune heterogeneity, with CD8-predominant tumor T cells versus CD4-predominant blood; IHC/Xenium confirmed CD3+ and CD8+ infiltration. Early data support biopsy–immunotherapy–resection feasibility and suggest treatment-associated immune remodeling. With multicenter expansion, Stage 1 is expected to complete accrual by SNO and provide integrated safety, flow, IHC, Xenium, CODEX, and 3D reconstruction data across tumor compartments to prioritize biomarkers for Stage 2.

papers.abstract: Abstract H3K27M-diffuse midline glioma (DMG) is an aggressive primary brain tumor with a poor prognosis and limited treatment options. The imipridone ONC201 has shown promise in phase I/II clinical trials and recently became the first FDA-approved systemic therapy for H3K27M-DMG. However, the response rate of H3K27M-DMG to ONC201 remains variable, with many patients not responding to the drug. Therefore, we aimed to investigate mechanisms underlying differential response to ONC201 in H3K27M-DMG. 11 primary patient-derived H3K27M-DMG cell lines were cultured and treated with ONC201. Cell viability was assessed after 72 hours using the CellTiterGlo assay. Protein and histone lysates were collected for immunoblotting. RNA sequencing was performed in 4 cell lines (2 responders vs 2 non-responders) and differential gene expression was analyzed with DESeq2 and Gene Set Enrichment Analysis. Established gene signatures were quantified using a robust z-score method. We found differential sensitivities to ONC201 across our cell lines (median IC50: 3.36uM, range: 1.53-23.69uM). We didn’t find an association between TCA cycle enzymes and H3K27me3 levels post-treatment and sensitivity to the drug. Among upregulated genes, 146 genes were consistently upregulated (p-adjusted < 0.05) across all 4 cell lines, and 71 genes were consistently downregulated. Among sensitive cell lines, PI3K-associated genes were selectively upregulated, while ribosomal RNA pathways were downregulated. In resistant cell lines, DNA damage response pathways were uniquely downregulated. Gene signature scoring based on scRNA-seq-derived H3K27M-DMG signatures stratified the sensitive and resistant cell lines via hierarchical clustering, revealing higher OPC/OC-like signatures on the sensitive cell lines. H3K27M-DMG cell lines demonstrate shared and distinct transcriptional responses to ONC201 associated with treatment sensitivity. These findings identify potential resistance mechanisms and biomarkers that may help identify patients who may respond better to ONC201, and also potential combination therapies.

papers.abstract: Abstract Introduction H3K27 mutant(H3K27M) tumors are the most common type of diffuse midline gliomas and are lethal childhood tumors with a median survival of less than 12 months. Standard upfront therapy is radiation alone, yet these tumors exhibit resistance to radiation, leading to rapid recurrence and significant neurological morbidity and death. As radiation kills tumor cells by inducing DNA double-strand breaks, rapid DNA repair is a known mechanism of RT resistance in other gliomas. However, the interactions mediating efficient DNA repair, radiation resistance, and recurrence are not well understood. Our goal was to identify mediators of treatment resistance in H3K27M tumors for therapeutic targeting to improve survival. Methods We developed an in vivo recurrence model to assess mediators of treatment resistance. Bulk RNA, single cell RNA, and spatial transcriptomics analyses were used to determine drivers of resistance, and genes of interest were mechanistically assessed for their role in resistance using genetic knockdown, DNA repair assays, colony formation assays, and in vivo patient-derived xenograft models. Results We determined that H3K27M epigenetic reprogramming drives loss of H3K27-tri-methylation at the THY1 locus resulting in consistent upregulation of THY1. We demonstrate that THY1 signaling activates Fyn which drives rapid repair of radiation-induced double-strand DNA damage-through the homologous recombination pathway. Knockdown of THY1 delays DNA repair in vitro and significantly improves survival of mouse models. Similarly, both genetic and pharmacological Fyn inhibition (with brain penetrant Saracatinib) phenocopies THY1 inhibition delays DNA repair and radiosensitizes tumors in vitro. When tested in vivo, Saracatinib significantly improves survival when combined with radiation. Conclusions We have uncovered that the Thy1-Fyn signaling cascade mediates rapid DNA repair and radiation resistance. Pharmacological Fyn inhibition successfully delays DNA repair in vitro and in vivo, radiosensitizes tumors, and significantly improves survival of mouse models. As Saracatinib is highly brain penetrant(0.5:1 Brain: Plasma ratio) and has demonstrated safety in Alzheimer’s clinical trials, it presents opportunities for clinical translation.

papers.abstract: Abstract Background H3K27-altered diffuse midline glioma (DMG), including diffuse intrinsic pontine glioma (DIPG), carries a median survival of 11 months. Since its recognition as a distinct molecular entity in 2016, diagnostic and therapeutic approaches have evolved, yet contemporary survival benchmarks remain limited. Here, we update survival outcomes for children with DMG. Methods PubMed and Embase were searched for English-language studies published between 2015 and 2025. Eligible studies included ≥9 patients aged ≤30 years with DIPG or DMG. Any therapeutic intervention was eligible. Eligible designs included RCTs, phase I–III trials, prospective single-arm studies, and retrospective cohorts. Studies were required to report extractable overall survival (OS) data at minimum. Two reviewers independently performed screening, data extraction, and quality assessment, with a third reviewer resolving discrepancies. Pooled median OS was calculated as the median of study-level median OS estimates across all included studies. For studies reporting confidence intervals, a supplementary inverse-variance weighted pooled estimate was also calculated. Results Of 191 studies identified, 23 duplicates were removed, yielding 168 for screening. Thirty-nine studies met inclusion criteria, comprising 1,832 patients. All studies included initial treatment with radiation; additional therapies evaluated across cohorts included chemotherapy, re-irradiation, immunotherapy, targeted therapy, novel agents, and combination regimens. The pooled median OS for the combined DIPG/DMG cohort was 13.1 months (IQR: 10.6–16.1 months). Among the 18 studies reporting confidence intervals (N = 1,197), the inverse-variance weighted pooled OS was 11.2 months (95% CI: 10.8–11.5 months). Conclusions Pooled survival outcomes demonstrate a modest improvement compared with historical benchmarks, with a median OS of 13.1 months. Molecular characterization was limited but increasingly reported over the study period. These data provide an updated baseline for future clinical trial design. Subgroup analyses by tumor location (thalamic vs. pontine vs other), treatment modality, and molecular profiling will be presented.

papers.abstract: Abstract Pharmacoscopy refers to an ex vivo real-time drug sensitivity profiling platform. The rationale for pharmacoscopy-based drug sensitivity testing on real-time patient surgical material is multiple: measuring drug response and sensitivity directly in real-time patient material, overcoming the problem of limited molecular biomarkers for established targeted therapeutic options and identifying effective drugs. Testing directly on patient material overcomes the limitations of patient-derived cell cultures, organoids, and patient xenografts, as their prolonged culture times risk cellular adaptations and clonal selection that alter drug sensitivity. Pharmacoscopy maintains the tumor cell composition, including bystander cells or tumor microenvironment, and limits cell culture to 24 hours. The EViDENCE-BM PCY System, providing results within 5 to 7 days, measures drug responses on a single-cell and on a high-content level, uniquely allowing to measure the drug sensitivity of tumor cells, and to compare it to the drug cytotoxicity on healthy cells from the same patient. The aim of the EViDENCE-BM study (NCT 06620380) is to generate preliminary data regarding superiority of the personalized pharmacoscopy-guided approach, in patients with brain metastases from solid tumors with an indication for surgery, and limited therapeutic systemic options according to the treating physician. Adult patients with limited systemic therapeutic options and an indication for surgery for brain metastasis are enrolled. Targeted therapy options should have been exhausted. Any type of primary cancer is allowed. This is a selection design, 3:1 randomized, non-comparative study, of a pharmacoscopy-guided approach (experimental arm) or standard non-pharmacoscopy-guided approach (control arm). The randomization happens prior to the surgery. The primary objective of EViDENCE-BM is to assess whether there is superiority of overall survival in a pharmacoscopy-guided arm compared to what would be expected with a standard non-pharmacoscopy-guided approach. Up to 56 agents are tested in the pharmacoscopy arm. Currently, 11 out of 102 patients have been enrolled at one center. Two new sites will be opened in the next weeks.

papers.abstract: Abstract Glioblastoma remains a highly aggressive malignancy with frequent recurrence and poor post-recurrence outcomes. Oncolytic immunovirotherapy is emerging as a promising strategy to overcome the immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment. DNX-2440, an oncolytic adenovirus armed with OX40 ligand, is designed to enhance antitumor immune responses and is currently being evaluated in a phase I clinical trial in recurrent glioblastoma. In this open-label, single-center, dose-escalation study, patients with first or second recurrence of GBM received a single intratumoral injection of DNX-2440. The treatment was well tolerated, with no dose-limiting toxicities observed and an acceptable safety profile. Preliminary evidence of clinical benefit, including tumor reduction and prolonged survival, has been observed in a subset of patients. To investigate systemic immune dynamics associated with treatment response, we analyzed 36 longitudinal bulk RNA-seq samples from peripheral blood lymphocytes (PBLs) obtained from 12 treated patients. Immune cell populations inferred by deconvolution were validated by flow cytometry. We applied a novel reference-free computational framework trained on single-cell data and benchmarked results against CIBERSORTx. Longitudinal immune profiling identified survival-associated immune states in peripheral blood that were not explained by clinical variables alone. Patients with improved survival exhibited a higher relative abundance of B cells compared to NK cells. Differential expression and longitudinal analyses highlighted genes including AREG, PCDH9, and FCRL1 as key contributors to survival-associated separation, with several top-loading genes linked to B cell function. These findings suggest that variation within the B cell compartment may influence response to DNX-2440 and support the use of peripheral blood immune profiling as a noninvasive approach for monitoring and biomarker discovery in recurrent GBM.

papers.abstract: Abstract Glioblastoma (GBM) remains the most lethal primary brain malignancy, with recurrence carrying a dismal prognosis and limited therapeutic options. Chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T cell therapy has shown encouraging early clinical activity, but determinants of response remain poorly understood. We performed longitudinal single-cell profiling of cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) and tumor tissue from patients with recurrent GBM treated with intracerebroventricular bivalent CAR T cells targeting amplified wtEGFR and IL13Rα2 in two University of Pennsylvania clinical trials. These included a phase 1 recurrent GBM study (NCT05660369, n = 18 patients) and a window-of-opportunity arm enabling on-treatment tumor tissue acquisition at peak immune activation (NCT07209241, n = 4 patients). CAR T cells robustly activated across patients, acquiring cytotoxic and exhaustion-associated transcriptional programs relative to the infusion product. However, therapeutic response was not associated with measured features of the infusion product or the magnitude of CAR T activation. Instead, response was significantly associated with remodeling of the endogenous immune compartment. Responders exhibited early expansion of cytotoxic NK populations, particularly CD56dimCD16pos states, detectable in CSF as early as day 7 and strongly associated with favorable progression-free survival. In contrast, Tregs expanded in both abundance and clonal dominance, inversely associated with tumor size reduction. CAR T infusion also induced a shift toward complement-associated immunosuppressive myeloid states across patients. Notably, all three immune remodeling dynamics were dose-dependent. Analysis of post-infusion tumor tissue further revealed adaptive malignant cell state transitions toward mesenchymal-like programs, alongside transcriptional changes consistent with physical barrier formation and metabolic immune resistance. These malignant adaptation programs were recapitulated in patient-derived GBM organoids following exposure to EGFR-targeted CAR T cells. These findings identify endogenous immune remodeling and tumor adaptation as key determinants of response and resistance to CAR T therapy in recurrent GBM, supporting rational combinatorial therapeutic strategies.

papers.abstract: Abstract Glioblastoma remains resistant to immunotherapy, motivating strategies that improve tumor-specific T-cell priming. ETAPA (NCT05283109) evaluated P30-EPS, a peptide vaccine linking class I tumor-associated antigens (cytomegalovirus pp65, Survivin, EphA2) to the universal class II tetanus toxoid epitope P30, to recruit CD4+ T-cell help and improve CD8+ priming. Adults with newly diagnosed MGMT-unmethylated glioblastoma (n = 18; 13M/5F; median age 61 [36–81], n = 17; median KPS 80 [70–90]) received up to seven post-radiation vaccinations with Hiltonol (TLR3 agonist, 20 μg/kg) plus P30-EPS at 300 μg (n = 6) or 400 μg (n = 12). PBMCs underwent IFN-γ ELISPOT, spectral flow cytometry, and 5′ single-cell TCR sequencing; paired baseline/on-treatment tumors underwent Xenium (5100 genes) and CODEX (60 markers) where available. Treatment was well tolerated; all treatment-related adverse events grade ≤2. Median PFS/OS were 9.7/15.3 months. In PBMCs, antigen-specific IFN-γ responses occurred in 11 patients, with stronger recall at 400 μg. Longer PFS was associated with higher baseline naïve CD4+ T-cell frequencies and fewer CD45RA+CCR7− effector-memory subsets, suggesting that preservation of a less differentiated CD4+ compartment supports effective vaccine-induced immunity. PBMC single-cell TCR sequencing showed greater clonotype expansion than a standard chemoradiation cohort (NCT05069597), consistent with memory formation. Xenium analysis of matched baseline/on-treatment cases (n = 8 tumors) suggested longer PFS was associated with greater adaptive immune infiltration and organization. One longer-PFS/OS tumor showed expansion of an endothelial-enriched niche occupying 56% of tissue, with increased central memory T cells, B cells, and Tertiary Lymphoid Structure (TLS)-like colocalization of T cells, B cells, CCL19, and CXCL13. Another longer-PFS tumor showed retroviral genes colocalizing with T and B cells in TLS-like regions. In contrast, a short-PFS/OS post-vaccine tumor showed astrocyte-like tumor and hypoxic TAM niches with minimal lymphoid infiltration. ETAPA met safety objectives and supports P30 linkage to enhance cytotoxic and memory T-cell responses and inform epitope-linked antigen-targeted vaccines.

papers.abstract: Abstract Background Natural killer (NK) cells have therapeutic potential in glioblastoma by recognizing multiple antigens on glioma stem cells through germ-line encoded receptors without requiring HLA antigen presentation or chimeric antigen receptor engineering. NK cells frequently infiltrate glioblastoma suggesting a role in tumor immune surveillance. Deletion of the TGFβ receptor 2 (TGF-βR2) and the glucocorticoid receptor (NR3C1) genes may protect NK cells from tumoral and iatrogenic immunosuppression. In this Phase I trial, we hypothesized that intratumoral delivery of umbilical cord blood (CB)-derived NK cells with multiplex CRISPR-based knock-down of TGF-βR2 and NR3C1 would be safe and would favorably modulate the tumor microenvironment. Methods Eligibility criteria included recurrent grade 4 IDH wild-type GBM patients, age > 18 yrs, and candidacy for intratumoral Ommaya catheter insertion. Primary objective was to evaluate the safety of CB NK TGF-βR2-/NR3C1- delivered intratumorally and to evaluate the immunological phenotype and anti-tumor function of these cells. Additional endpoints included progression free survival (PFS) and overall survival (OS). Results In 6 patients, median PFS was 4.2 months (95% confidence interval 1.8, NA) and median OS from treatment start was 11.8 months (9.4, NA). Incidence of grade 3 AEs was 67% with 17% possibly treatment related. Four of 6 patients underwent re-resection after treatment. Higher percentages of CD45+ cells, NK cells (including donor-derived NK cells), CD8+ T cells and myeloid cells were seen after treatment. Post-treatment tissue revealed enhanced macrophage and CD8+ T cell activation as well as polarization to M1-like macrophages. In 4 paired specimens, spatial transcriptomics revealed the interaction of infused NK cells within the tumor microenvironment. Conclusions The intratumoral delivery of CB NK TGF-βR2-/NR3C1- in this cohort of recurrent glioblastoma patients was safe. Post treatment analysis reveals persistence of donor-derived CB-NK cells within tumor tissue, increased T cell infiltration, and favorable remodeling of the myeloid tumor microenvironment.

papers.abstract: Abstract Meningiomas are the most common primary intracranial tumors and are 2-4 times more common in females compared with males. Progestins increase the risk of meningioma, and progestin-induced or pregnancy-associated meningiomas can regress as serum progestogen levels normalize. The mechanisms that underlie sex differences and progestogen signaling in meningioma are unknown. Here we show that sex hormone interaction with PGRMC1, a progesterone binding protein, regulates the activity of RNA processing proteins to drive meningioma sex differences. Using mass spectrometry-based proteomics to analyze 603 meningiomas with copy number alteration, DNA methylation, gene expression, histological, and clinical data, we demonstrate that meningiomas are enriched in RNA processing proteins that are not identified by genomic approaches. Meningioma molecular architecture is conserved across vertebrate species, and we validate our proteomic findings using 79 meningiomas from dogs. Using CRISPRi screening, machine learning, CLIP sequencing, long-read RNA sequencing, and RNA stability assays, we show that RNA processing proteins FXR1 and RBM39 drive meningioma growth in response to progestogens by binding and stabilizing progesterone receptor transcript (PGR) to express progesterone receptor protein (PR). Immunoprecipitation mass spectrometry and structure-function studies show progestogens release FXR1 and RBM39 from PGRMC1 to stabilize PGR and drive expression of PGR and PR. Testosterone and the small molecule AG205 bind to PGRMC1, stabilize interactions with FXR1 and RBM39, and reduce PGR and PR expression. We find that progestogens signal through this pathway to drive meningioma growth in female mice and in male mice after testosterone depletion through castration, and that testosterone, AG205, and RBM39 degradation with the small molecule indisulam block meningioma growth. Using ChIP and spatial transcriptomic sequencing, we define a gene expression biomarker of PR activity. These findings reveal therapeutic strategies that may improve outcomes for patients and elucidate an estrogen receptor-independent mechanism of PR expression that underlies sex differences in meningioma.

papers.abstract: Introduction Simultaneous presentation of secondary hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis (HLH) with de novo acute myeloid leukemia (AML) is uncommon. KMT2A rearrangements, present in approximately 2–7% of de-novo AML, confer aggressive biology, and HLH at the initial diagnosis of KMT2A -rearranged AML is rare. Case-presentation A 47-year-old man presented with influenza-A infection, pancytopenia (WBC 1.08×10³/µL, hemoglobin 10.4 g/dL, platelets 147×10³/µL), acute kidney and hepatic dysfunction, disseminated intravascular coagulation, hypertriglyceridemia (517 mg/dL), hyperferritinemia (73, 776 µg/L), and splenomegaly meeting HLH-2004 criteria. Bone-marrow biopsy revealed 80% blasts with monocytic differentiation and hemophagocytosis, along with KMT2A rearrangement. Treatment with high-dose dexamethasone and 7 + 3 induction chemotherapy achieved MRD-negative complete remission. He received two cycles of high-dose cytarabine consolidation followed by allogeneic stem cell transplantation and remains in remission at 26 months. Conclusion To our knowledge, this is the first reported case of HLH occurring concurrently with de novo KMT2A-rearranged AML at initial diagnosis. This case highlights the importance of early recognition and concurrent management of HLH and KMT2A -r AML to prevent rapid clinical deterioration and achieve durable remission.

papers.abstract: Background Mucinous breast carcinoma (MBC) is a rare histological type of breast cancer. Mucinous breast carcinoma with micropapillary pattern (MPMC) is defined by the presence of any micropapillary architecture. This retrospective cohort study aimed to evaluate the prognostic significance of the micropapillary pattern on disease-free survival in patients with mucinous breast carcinoma. Methods We conducted a retrospective analysis of all mucinous breast carcinoma cases diagnosed between 2005 and 2024. Clinicopathological parameters, treatment modalities, and survival outcomes were collected and analyzed. Prognostic factors were evaluated using a prespecified reduced Cox model as the primary analysis. Because limited DFS events occurred, all multivariable estimates were considered exploratory. DeepSurv was used as a supplementary exploratory analysis to capture potential nonlinear relationships. Results A total of 344 mucinous breast carcinoma cases were included, among which 65 patients (18.9%) exhibited micropapillary pattern. Kaplan–Meier analysis showed significantly worse disease-free survival in MPMC patients (11 events vs. 6 events), with 5-year disease-free survival (DFS) rates of 76.7% and 97.3%, respectively ( p < 0.001). In the prespecified reduced Cox model, the micropapillary pattern was associated with worse DFS (HR 8.17; 95% CI 2.88–21.76; p < 0.001). However, because only 17 DFS events occurred, this estimate was imprecise and exploratory. In sensitivity analyses, the full model yielded HR 8.05 (95% CI 2.90–22.37) and Firth’s penalized likelihood correction yielded HR 10.74 (95% CI 3.52–32.83). Hypercellularity was also associated with worse DFS (HR 7.55; 95% CI 2.61–21.85). In the supplementary exploratory DeepSurv analysis, the model captured potential nonlinear relationships and achieved a C-index of 0.858, with AUCs of 0.804, 0.878, and 0.826 for 1-, 3-, and 5-year DFS, respectively, and a Brier score of 0.022. However, these performance estimates may be optimistic because only 17 DFS events occurred; DeepSurv was therefore considered exploratory and not clinically validated. Conclusions MPMCs exhibit more aggressive tumor behavior and are associated with worse prognosis, with hypercellularity also identified as a significant poor prognostic factor. These findings suggest that MPMC may represent a higher-risk subgroup requiring closer surveillance. However, treatment implications should still be interpreted cautiously and require prospective validation.

papers.abstract: Background Research on rectal neuroendocrine neoplasms (R-NENs) has grown, but the development of this site-specific literature and the consistency of its main patterns across databases have not been examined together. Methods We mapped English-language articles and reviews from the Web of Science Core Collection (WoSCC), then used separately screened Scopus and PubMed records to compare publication trends, leading countries, and prespecified clinical themes. Author keywords and Keywords Plus were normalized and deduplicated within records. Results The primary WoSCC corpus included 875 publications. Of these, 803 met the direct title-and-abstract rule used for validation; the corresponding Scopus and PubMed sets contained 1,018 and 703 records. Annual output was strongly correlated across databases (Pearson r=0.979–0.992), although record overlap was moderate (Jaccard=0.531–0.545). Country and theme ranks showed partial agreement, while their absolute frequencies varied. Across time, the literature moved from historical ‘carcinoid’ terminology toward endoscopic resection, pathological risk, prognosis, and decisions after local treatment. Conclusion The analysis maps how R-NEN research has developed and where further clinical studies are needed. Cross-database agreement supports the overall growth pattern and some broad rankings, but it does not establish the validity of any treatment strategy.

papers.abstract: Diffuse leptomeningeal glioneuronal tumor (DLGNT) represents a rare central nervous system neoplasm predominantly observed in pediatric patients. Most cases pursue an indolent clinical course; nevertheless, a small subset demonstrates high-grade histology together with craniospinal dissemination and carries a dismal prognosis. We describe a 6-year-old girl presenting with recurrent vomiting and obstructive hydrocephalus. Initial neuroimaging revealed cerebellar cystic lesions and diffuse leptomeningeal enhancement, which was initially misinterpreted as infectious meningoencephalitis. Tumor biopsy was declined by the patient’s family at initial consultation, and ventriculoperitoneal shunt placement was performed for hydrocephalus relief. One year after shunt surgery, craniospinal magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) documented substantial tumor progression, with corpus callosum infiltration and vertebral body signal abnormalities. Subsequent biopsy established the diagnosis of DLGNT with high-grade histological features, with a Ki-67 proliferation index of approximately 80%. DNA-methylation profiling assigned the tumor to the DLGNT-MC2 molecular subclass. Additional molecular findings included KIAA1549::BRAF gene fusion, 1p deletion, 1q gain, and 17q gain, with an intact 19q and no 1p/19q codeletion. The child received eight cycles of carboplatin, etoposide, and vincristine (CEV) chemotherapy. Nine months after completing treatment, whole-neuroaxis contrast-enhanced MRI (brain and entire spine) showed no residual or recurrent enhancing lesions in either the brain or spine. Neurological function remained stable, and no further seizure episodes occurred. Treatment-related adverse events were confined to grade 2 myelosuppression and mild gastrointestinal intolerance, which were managed by supportive care measures. Our case suggests that risk-adapted CEV chemotherapy may serve as a reasonable upfront therapeutic option for unresectable, aggressive MC2-subtype DLGNT, achieving a short-term complete radiological response. Extended clinical and radiological surveillance is mandatory to validate long-term disease control.

papers.abstract: Objective This study aims to synthesize the evidence and appraise available evidence on the management of radiotherapy-induced digestive symptoms in head and neck cancer (HNC) patients to support clinical assessment and intervention. Methods Evidence was retrieved from evidence-based resources and databases following the “6S” model. The literature quality assessment followed the Appraisal of Guidelines for Research and Evaluation (AGREE II) for guidelines, AMSTAR-2 for systematic reviews, and Joanna Briggs Institute (JBI) Evidence-Based Health Care Center’s quality evaluation tool for expert opinions and expert consensus articles. Quality evaluation, evidence extraction and summary were performed by two main researchers, combined with the advice from a senior nursing expert specialized in oncology care. Results A total of 21 pieces of literature were included, consisting of 6 guidelines, 6 expert consensuses, and 9 systematic reviews. Key evidence (n=37) was synthesized across six domains: oral mucositis, xerostomia, dysgeusia, nutritional management, dysphagia, nausea and vomiting. Conclusions This evidence summary summarizes evidence-based strategies for managing digestive symptoms in HNC patients undergoing radiotherapy, providing clinicians and nurses with a reference for assessment and intervention. Implementation should be adapted to specific clinical contexts, patient preferences, and professional expertise to enhance utility in a real-world setting. Registration This study has been registered on the Fudan University Center for Evidence-based Nursing (registration No. ES20246039).

papers.abstract: Colorectal cancer (CRC) remains a leading cause of cancer incidence and mortality worldwide, and metastatic disease responds poorly to conventional surgery, chemotherapy, and targeted therapy. Antibody-drug conjugates (ADCs) link monoclonal antibodies to cytotoxic payloads through chemical linkers, enabling antigen-specific delivery, intracellular payload release, bystander killing, and Fc-mediated immune effects. ADC efficacy and safety depend on target antigen selection, antibody design, payload choice, linker stability, and internalization efficiency. This narrative review, based on literature and trial data available up to February 2026, summarizes the CRC treatment landscape, ADC mechanisms and component optimization, and clinical progress of ADCs targeting HER2, HER3, TROP-2, CEACAM5, and c-MET. No ADC has been approved specifically for CRC; trastuzumab deruxtecan has tumor-agnostic accelerated approval for HER2 IHC 3+ solid tumors and may cover eligible patients with metastatic CRC. Early trials show promising activity but substantial hematologic, gastrointestinal, hepatic, and interstitial lung disease toxicity, reflecting a narrow therapeutic window. We discuss challenges including target specificity, off-target toxicity, drug resistance, and linker stability, and outline future directions such as probody-drug conjugates, bispecific and dual-payload ADCs, novel payloads, and bioorthogonal linkers to support precision therapy for CRC.

papers.abstract: Immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs) have transformed cancer treatment, but approved schedules do not establish whether treatment intensity should remain constant as tumor burden, immunity, toxicity, and response evolve. Continued treatment after durable response may add toxicity and treatment burden while providing uncertain incremental benefit. This structured narrative review examines adaptive immunotherapy dosing: prespecified, state-dependent modification of dose, interval, or duration, including interruption and resumption. Exposure–response plateaus and time-varying clearance support investigating alternative regimens but do not establish clinical equivalence. Evidence on discontinuation remains disease- and regimen-specific, precluding generalization from melanoma to non-small cell lung cancer or other settings. Response- and biomarker-guided strategies have prospective support in defined settings, including response-driven adjuvant therapy in melanoma and circulating tumor DNA–selected adjuvant therapy in muscle-invasive bladder cancer. These advances do not validate repeated biomarker-guided adjustment of ICI dose, interval, or duration. Most candidate longitudinal biomarkers show outcome associations without demonstrated utility for dosing adaptation. Artificial intelligence and computational models may integrate serial data but require prospective evaluation, external validation, and safeguards against unsafe individual predictions. Dynamic treatment regimes and adaptive trial methods offer tools for evaluating complete policies, with attention to endpoints, patient preferences, assay performance, equity, and regulation. The proposed conceptual framework organizes these requirements for prospective investigation; it is not a clinical algorithm. Trials must establish whether matching treatment intensity to an evolving clinical state preserves efficacy while reducing toxicity and burden and improving quality of life. Approved regimens and validated disease-specific strategies remain the clinical benchmark.

papers.abstract: Background Contrast-enhanced CT remains the staging workhorse in metastatic colorectal cancer but under-detects small hypovascular colorectal liver metastases (CRLM) relative to MRI. Photon-counting detector CT (PCCT) offers higher spatial resolution and lower electronic noise, yet clinical evidence on lesion detection is scarce. Methods In this single-centre, intra-patient reader study, 15 patients with colorectal cancer and hepatic metastases underwent both energy-integrating detector CT (EID-CT) and PCCT within the same month with each scanner’s routine protocol (PCCT: 140 kV, 0.4 mm sections; EID-CT: 100 kV, 1.0 mm sections), during documented oncological stability, plus contrast-enhanced liver MRI. A consensus panel defined an MRI-anchored reference map of 46 metastases. Three radiologists of differing experience independently reviewed both arms in randomised order, blinded to scanner type, clinical data and reference standard, without cue to lesion number or location. Detection, conspicuity and diagnostic confidence were scored per reference lesion. PCCT was read at conventional-equivalent monoenergies (65–70 keV). Results Per-lesion sensitivity against the MRI-anchored reference was 138/138 reads (100%; 95% CI 97.3–100) for PCCT versus 122/138 (88.4%; 95% CI 82.0–92.7) for EID-CT; all 16 discordant reads favoured PCCT (exact McNemar P < 0.001; patient-clustered bootstrap difference +11.5 points, 95% CI 1.6–24.1). Eight of 46 metastases (17.4%) were missed on EID-CT and none on PCCT. The complete metastatic burden was reproduced in 45/45 patient-level PCCT reads versus 37/45 (82.2%) on EID-CT. Composite conspicuity was 4.57 ± 0.48 versus 3.53 ± 0.88 (+1.04, patient-clustered 95% CI 0.72–1.33; P < 0.001) and diagnostic confidence 4.28 ± 0.53 versus 3.62 ± 0.87 (+0.66, 95% CI 0.42–0.89; P < 0.001). The confidence gain was smaller for the least experienced reader (mixed-effects model P = 0.004). False-positive findings were not recorded, so specificity could not be assessed. Conclusion In this preliminary comparison of two routine clinical protocols, PCCT showed higher per-lesion sensitivity than EID-CT, identifying every reference metastasis, and improved conspicuity and confidence, even without low-keV optimisation. Because section thickness, tube voltage, pitch and kernel differed between protocols, the advantage reflects the PCCT system as a whole rather than the detector alone. PCCT may narrow the CT–MRI detection gap in CRLM, a hypothesis requiring confirmation in larger free-response studies with matched reconstruction parameters.

papers.abstract: Background Reliable comparison of deep learning models for oral histopathology is hindered by morphological overlap between diagnostic classes and by substantial variation in data partitioning, optimization, and evaluation across published studies. We therefore performed a large controlled benchmark to examine predictive performance, training stability, statistical uncertainty, and computational efficiency under a unified framework. Methods Thirty-one architectures from nine model families were evaluated on the three-class ORCHID and P-NDB-UFES datasets using a common downstream training, checkpoint-selection, and testing protocol. ORCHID was repartitioned at the patient/tissue-slide-group level, while the predefined 627-patch P-NDB-UFES test subset was retained unchanged because complete patient provenance was unavailable. Leading models were repeated across five random seeds. ORCHID uncertainty was estimated by cluster-aware resampling over 14 independent test groups. Evaluation included macro-F1, AUROC, AUPRC, MCC, class-specific errors, parameter count, GFLOPs, GPU forward-pass efficiency, and qualitative Grad-CAM analysis. Results MobileViTv2–150 achieved the highest primary ORCHID macro-F1 (0.9428), whereas DeiT III-Base/16 led P-NDB-UFES (0.9037). Across five seeds, the highest mean macro-F1 shifted to Swin-Large on ORCHID (0.9348 ± 0.0110) and DeiT III-Small/16 on P-NDB-UFES (0.9031 ± 0.0091). Cluster-aware ORCHID intervals overlapped among the leading models, and several compact or intermediate-scale networks matched substantially larger architectures with lower computational demand. Residual errors concentrated at morphologically difficult class boundaries and included high-confidence misclassifications. Conclusions No architecture consistently dominated both diagnostic tasks. Model selection should emphasize class-balanced performance, repeated-run stability, independence-aware uncertainty, computational cost, and clinically relevant failure patterns rather than a single-run ranking.

papers.abstract: Background Previous studies have implicated CKLF-like MARVEL transmembrane domain-containing 3 (CMTM3) in glioma progression and have demonstrated effects on glioma-cell proliferation and invasion. However, its relationship with cellular composition of the glioblastoma (GBM) microenvironment and adaptive endoplasmic reticulum (ER)-stress responses remains incompletely characterized. We therefore investigated the cellular context of CMTM3 expression and its association with selected unfolded protein response (UPR)-related signals in GBM, together with complementary functional validation in GBM cells. Methods GEO, TCGA, and Human Protein Atlas datasets were integrated with single-cell RNA sequencing, survival analysis, protein-interaction and correlation analyses, functional enrichment, and immune-infiltration profiling. CMTM3 was silenced in U87 and U251 cells, followed by migration, colony-formation, CCK-8, and Western blot assays. Endoplasmic reticulum (ER) stress was induced with tunicamycin (2 μg/mL, 24 h). Results In the legacy TCGA glioma cohorts, CMTM3 expression was associated with higher WHO grade, IDH-wild-type status, and older age, whereas higher CMTM3 expression in TCGA-GBM was associated with shorter overall survival. In the vascular-enriched single-cell dataset, CMTM3 expression was detected across multiple populations and was prominent in endothelial and mural/perivascular clusters. CMTM3 knockdown impaired migration, reduced clonogenic capacity, and decreased cellular metabolic activity. GO/KEGG analysis highlighted protein processing in the ER. Under tunicamycin treatment, CMTM3-depleted cells showed lower p-PERK, ATF4, and XBP1s protein levels than control cells, whereas BiP and CHOP did not differ significantly between the treated groups. However, two-way ANOVA revealed no significant CMTM3 knockdown × tunicamycin interaction for any of the five examined proteins. Conclusion Our findings extend previous observations on CMTM3 in glioma by identifying associations with selected UPR-related protein levels under tunicamycin exposure and to vascular and stromal features of the GBM microenvironment. These results provide a basis for further investigation of the cellular and stress-response context of CMTM3 in GBM.

papers.abstract: Background The prognostic impact of KIT mutations in pediatric acute myeloid leukemia (AML) with RUNX1::RUNX1T1 remains controversial. Methods We conducted a systematic literature search of PubMed, Embase, Cochrane Library, Web of Science Core Collection, and China National Knowledge Infrastructure (CNKI) databases from their inception to November 26, 2025. Two investigators independently performed the literature search and study selection using predefined keywords. Eligible studies were screened according to inclusion and exclusion criteria, followed by data extraction. A meta-analysis was performed using R software. Results A total of 9 studies comprising 2103 patients were included in the final meta-analysis. The results demonstrated that KIT mutations were associated with inferior event-free survival (EFS) in pediatric AML patients with RUNX1::RUNX1T1 (HR = 2.69, 95% CI: 1.44–5.01), as well as inferior overall survival (OS) (HR = 3.06, 95% CI: 1.64–5.69). Conclusion In conclusion, KIT mutations are an adverse prognostic factor in pediatric acute myeloid leukemia with RUNX1::RUNX1T1 . papers.abstract: Background Go-Ichi-Ni-San complex subunit 4 (GINS4) has been implicated in regulating ferroptosis, but evidence regarding thyroid cancer is scarce. This study aimed to investigate the effects of GINS4 on ferroptosis and the underlying mechanisms in thyroid cancer. Methods Human thyroid cancer cell lines TPC-1 and IHH4 were transfected with GINS4-specific siRNA. Ferroptosis inhibition and p53 pathway validation were performed using ferrostatin-1 (Ferr-1) and pifithrin-α (PFT-α), respectively. Protein-protein interaction (PPI) network analysis was performed to investigate the potential association between GINS4 and ferroptosis-related markers. Results GINS4 knockdown promoted ferroptosis in thyroid cancer cell lines, as reflected by increased reactive oxygen species (ROS), malondialdehyde (MDA), and Fe 2+ levels, as well as reduced mitochondrial membrane potential (MMP). The addition of Ferr-1 reversed the effects of GINS4 knockdown on ferroptosis in thyroid cancer cell lines, suggesting that GINS4 knockdown-induced cell death was mainly attributable to ferroptosis. PPI network analysis identified p53 as a potential hub molecule in the GINS4-associated ferroptosis network, with SLC7A11 and GPX4 as key ferroptosis-related downstream proteins. Western blot analysis confirmed that GINS4 knockdown increased p53 while decreasing SLC7A11 and GPX4 in thyroid cancer cell lines. PFT-α reversed the effects of GINS4 knockdown on the p53/SLC7A11/GPX4 pathway and ferroptosis in thyroid cancer cell lines, indicating that the p53/SLC7A11/GPX4 pathway might contribute to GINS4 knockdown-mediated ferroptosis. Conclusion GINS4 knockdown facilitates ferroptosis through the p53/SLC7A11/GPX4 pathway in thyroid cancer cell lines.

papers.abstract: BRCA1 and BRCA2 germline deleterious variants are associated with a high risk of hereditary breast and ovarian cancer. The presence of pathogenic variants in both genes in the same individual (double heterozygosity) is rare and often associated with distinct clinical characteristics. We report a rare case of double heterozygosity involving a novel combination of pathogenic variants. A 40-year-old woman was diagnosed with stage IIIA invasive ductal carcinoma of the right breast. Histopathology revealed a grade 2, ER-positive (100%), PR-positive (70%), HER2-negative (FISH), high-proliferation Luminal B tumor. She received neoadjuvant dose-dense AC chemotherapy. Germline testing via next-generation sequencing identified two pathogenic variants: NM_007294.4 (BRCA1) :c.2105del (p.Lys701_Leu702ins*) in exon 11 and NM_000059.4 (BRCA2): c.1763_1766del (p.Asn588Serfs*25) in exon 10, both heterozygous. The patient reported a strong maternal family history of breast cancer. A systematic review of the literature and databases (PubMed, ClinVar, BRCA Exchange) did not reveal any previous clinical reports of this specific variant combination. Cases of double heterozygosity remain rare (<0.5% of BRCA carriers), and clinical data on variant-specific co-occurrence is limited. This case represents the first known report of a patient carrying both NM_007294.4 ( BRCA1 ): c.2105del (p.Lys701_Leu702ins*) and NM_000059.4 ( BRCA2 ): c.1763_1766del (p.Asn588Serfs*25) pathogenic variants. The findings contribute valuable information to the spectrum of hereditary breast cancer and underscore the importance of comprehensive genetic testing, especially in patients with strong family histories.

papers.abstract: Dendritic cells (DCs) are central orchestrators of antitumor immunity, yet their therapeutic potential is constrained by dysfunction and inadequate activation within solid tumors. Here we report chimeric antigen receptor-engineered DCs (CAR-DCs) that prime T cells and reprogram the tumor microenvironment. We identify the intracellular domains of CLEC9A or LY75 (DEC205) as essential for functional CAR-DC activity, enabling enhanced antigen uptake and cross-presentation and driving T cell expansion and function. CARs incorporating the CLEC9A or DEC205 intracellular domains triggered SYK phosphorylation and downstream signaling. In both conventional and humanized mouse models, CAR-DC therapy suppressed tumor growth and promoted expansion of tumor-reactive T cells. These findings establish CAR-DCs as scalable and clinically translatable platforms for next-generation solid tumor immunotherapy.

papers.abstract: Epithelial stratification, the transition from a monolayer to a multilayer structure, occurs across a wide range of phenomena. Recent studies have identified several cell behaviors as triggers, including junctional tension, cell density and geometry, and topological defects. However, how these factors drive stratification throughout the entire epithelium remains poorly understood. Here, we show that epithelial stratification proceeds through a nucleation-and-growth mechanism. Combining cell culture with three-dimensional vertex modeling, we demonstrate that multilayer origins emerge in a dispersed manner and expand across the epithelium through disordered intermediate states. This transition is induced by a mechanical instability inherent in the foam-like geometry of the epithelium. Moreover, the nucleation-growth concept applies to embryonic skin development and intestinal cancer transformation. These findings conceptualize epithelial stratification as a form of structural transition governed by foam mechanics, offering a physical perspective on various epithelial developments.

papers.abstract: The maternal-fetal interface and the tumor microenvironment (TME) of gynecologic malignancies represent two immunological settings in which semi-allogeneic or neoantigen-bearing tissues must evade immune destruction. Although these contexts have traditionally been studied in isolation, accumulating evidence reveals that pregnancy and cancer deploy remarkably convergent mechanisms of immune evasion. This review synthesizes emerging data on shared immune checkpoint molecules, metabolic immunosuppression, immune cell remodeling, and hormonal orchestration that constitute an “onco-fetal” immune tolerance network. We focus on six checkpoint axes—B7-H4, PD-L1/PD-1, HLA-G, IDO, CD47-SIRPα, and Galectin-9/TIM-3—detailing their molecular mechanisms at both the decidua and gynecologic TME. The 2024 discovery that progesterone drives B7-H4 expression through a PR-P300-BRD4 transcriptional axis—first identified in trophoblasts and breast cancer cells and likely conserved across hormone-associated malignancies including gynecologic cancers—provides a conceptual anchor for this onco-fetal framework. Notably, breast cancer serves as a mechanistic reference model in this review, while our primary focus is on ovarian, endometrial, and cervical malignancies. We further examine convergent metabolic immunosuppression (tryptophan catabolism, adenosine signaling, glucose competition, arginine depletion), paralleled remodeling of regulatory T cells, myeloid-derived suppressor cells, macrophages, and exhausted T cells, and the hormonal nexus linking these processes. The therapeutic paradox—whereby immune checkpoint inhibition is essential for cancer treatment yet contraindicated in pregnancy—underscores the translational urgency of understanding these shared pathways. We discuss B7-H4-directed antibody-drug conjugates, CD47-SIRPα blockade, IDO pathway inhibition, and bispecific antibody strategies in gynecologic oncology, alongside single-cell and spatial transcriptomic technologies reshaping our understanding of both fields. This onco-fetal perspective offers a unifying framework for developing precision immunotherapies that selectively disrupt tumor immune tolerance while preserving physiological pregnancy tolerance.

papers.abstract: Background Approximately 20-40% of patients with metastatic non-small cell lung cancer (mNSCLC) present with Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group (ECOG) performance status (PS) 2, yet are systematically excluded from pivotal immunotherapy trials. Current guidelines recommend similar first-line regimens for PS0–1 and PS2 patients based on extrapolated data, creating clinical uncertainty. Methods This single-center, pragmatic pilot phase II study compares outcomes of standard first-line immunotherapy-based regimens between PS2 and PS0–1 patients with mNSCLC. Eligible patients receive NCCN-preferred regimens selected by treating providers per standard care. The primary outcome is 3-month progression-free survival (PFS), defined as the proportion without disease progression after four treatment cycles. Secondary outcomes include treatment-related adverse events and patient-reported quality of life changes. The study employs a non-inferiority design (margin –0.20 absolute difference in 3-month PFS proportion, α 0.05, 83% power) to assess whether PS2 patients achieve comparable early disease control to PS0–1 patients. Anticipated results We hypothesize that selected PS2 patients will demonstrate non-inferior 3-month PFS compared to PS0–1 patients when treated with standard immunotherapy-based regimens, with acceptable toxicity and quality of life outcomes. Conclusion This pragmatic trial addresses a critical evidence gap by prospectively evaluating whether performance status alone should preclude use of standard immunotherapy-based regimens in mNSCLC, providing data to inform shared decision-making for this underrepresented population. Clinical trial registration https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT04253964 , identifier NCT04253964.
